The Welsh MSS. Society,

Has been formed for the purpose of transcribing and printing the more important of the numerous Bardic and Historical Remains of Wales, still extant in the Principality, and other parts of the world, that have hitherto been allowed to continue in a state of obscurity, without any effective measures being adopted to lay their contents before the public, and secure them from the various accidents to which they are liable. In addition to the general decay which, from their perishable nature, these venerable relics have been for ages undergoing, whole collections have, within a short space of time, been destroyed by fire; and of those MSS. dispersed throughout the country, numbers known to have existed a few years ago, are now nowhere to be found.

Besides the interest which these ancient documents possess, as objects of antiquarian curiosity, and as contributing to the elucidation of British History, they have a claim to attention of a far more general character, as being intimately connected with the origin and progress of modern European Literature; for it is among the legends and traditions of the Welsh that many of the materials are to be found, which supplied the nations of the Continent with their earliest subjects of composition, and produced those highly imaginative works that continue to exercise so powerful an influence to the present day.

A great mass of historical information, relating to the thirteenth, fourteenth, and fifteenth centuries, is contained in the unpublished Poetry of Wales; from which an intimate acquaintance with the state of society during those periods may be obtained; the Welsh Bards being the chroniclers of the times in which they lived, and their Poems chiefly addressed to the leading men of the day. Besides Poetry, there is still existing unpublished a large collection of Prose, both Historical and Legendary; persons of affluence are therefore solicited to contribute larger Donations and Subscriptions, than are required by the Rules of the Society, in order to enable the Committee to proceed with greater rapidity in carrying on the publication of Manuscripts.

The first Work published by this Society was the Liber Landavensis, or Llyfr Teilo, comprising nearly 700 Royal 8vo. pages; gratuitously edited and translated by the late Rev. W. J. Rees, M.A., F.S.A. etc. Of this Work only a few copies remain available to persons becoming Members of the Society at £1 1s. 0d.

The second Work of the Society consisted of a Miscellaneous Selection of Ancient Welsh MSS. in prose and poetry, from the originals collected by the late Edward Williams, (Iolo Morganwg) for the purpose of forming a continuation of the Myvyrian Archaiology, and afterwards proposed to be used as materials for a New History of Wales. Edited with Notes and Translations, by his son, the late Taliesin ab Iolo, of Merthyr Tydfil. This work is of the same size and price as the Liber Landavensis, and a few copies remain still in the hands of the Publisher.

The third Work, The Heraldic Visitations of Wales and its Marches, during the reigns of Elizabeth and James I, in two Imperial 4to. Volumes, was printed under the gratuitous and able superintendence of its Editor, the late Sir Samuel Rush Meyrick, K.H., LL.D., F.S.A., etc. Of this Work only 240 copies were published, which were all taken up by Subscribers; it is therefore out of print and has become extremely scarce.

The Lives of Cambro British Saints was next published, from Ancient Welsh and Latin MSS. in the British Museum and elsewhere, comprising 680 pages Royal 8vo., and was gratuitously edited and translated by the late Rev. W. J. Rees, M.A., F.S.A., etc. Some copies of this Work are still to be had from the Publisher, price £1 1s. 0d. to persons becoming Members of the Society.

Rules of the Society.

I. That the objects of the Society shall be to procure copies of any interesting Manuscripts relating to Wales and the Marches thereof, and to publish them with English Translations and Notes.

II. That Subscribers of at least One Guinea annually become members of the Society.

III. That all Subscriptions being considered due for the ensuing year, notice must be sent to the Secretary, before the 1st of January, of any Member's intention to withdraw his name.

IV. That the Society's Publications are to appear yearly in parts or volumes, to be delivered free to Subscribers not in arrear with the subscriptions.

V. That there shall be only a limited number of copies printed of each Work beyond the number of Subscribers, which copies the Committee are empowered to dispose of to persons becoming annual subscribers.

VI. That the management of the affairs of the Society be vested in the Chairman and Committee, and that the funds of the Society be disbursed in payment of the necessary expenses incident to the production of the Works of the Society, and that the accounts of the receipts and expenditure be audited annually by two Members.

Subscribers' Names, Donations and Annual Subscriptions are requested to be forwarded to the Secretary, Mr. Griffith, 4, Sidmouth Place, Gray's Inn Road, London.

PREFACE.

Meddyginiaeth, or medicine, is counted as one of "the nine rural arts, known and practiced by the ancient Welsh people before they came to possess cities and sovereignty;" that is, before the time of Prydain ab Aedd Mawr, which is generally dated about a thousand years before the Christian era. In that distant period the priests and teachers of the people were the Gwyddoniaid, or men of knowledge, so called because they were regarded as the chief sources and channels of wisdom in the land. To these men is attributed the art of healing, which they appear to have practiced mainly, if not entirely, through the use of herbs. Indeed, Botanology, or knowledge of the nature and properties of plants, is listed as one of the three sciences that primarily occupied their attention — the other two being Theology and Astronomy, as shown by the following Triad:—

"The three pillars of knowledge with which the Gwyddoniaid were acquainted, and which they kept in memory from the beginning: the first, a knowledge of Divine things, and of such matters as relate to the worship of God and the respect due to goodness; the second, a knowledge of the course of the stars, their names and kinds, and the order of time; the third, a knowledge of the names and use of the herbs of the field, and of their practical application in medicine and in religious worship. These were preserved in the traditions of vocal song, and in the records of time, before there were Bards of degree and chair."†

* Myv. Arch. iii. p. 129.     † Llanover MS.

Most of the nations of antiquity pretended to derive the medical art immediately from their gods. It does not appear, however, that the Cymry went so far as to claim for it a divine origin, except in regard to its elementary principles, though the practice of it was confined to the priesthood. In this latter respect also they differed from many old and powerful races. The most ancient physicians we read of in history were those who embalmed the patriarch Jacob by order of his son Joseph. Moses describes these physicians as servants to Joseph, from which we can be sure they were not priests, for in that age the Egyptian priests were held in such high favour that they retained their liberty when, through a public calamity, all the rest of the people became slaves to the king. In Egypt, then, religion and medicine were not combined together. That the Jewish physicians as a class were absolutely distinct from the priests is also very certain; for when king Asa was diseased in his feet, "he sought not to the Lord, but to the physicians." It would appear that such was likewise the case with the heathens who dwelt near the Jews, as may be inferred from what is recorded of Ahaziah, king of Judah; when he sent messengers to enquire of Baal-zebub, god of Ekron, concerning his disease, he did not desire any remedy from him or his priest, but only to know whether he should recover or not.

But among the Cymry all branches of knowledge were centered indiscriminately in the Gwyddoniaid until the time of Prydain. In his reign these were divided into three orders: Bards, Druids, and Ovates.

Each having its peculiar duties as well as privileges. It was to the Ovate more especially that the studies and application of terrestrial and natural sciences, such as the one which now engages our attention, were entrusted.

In the Laws of Dyvnwal Moelmud, "medicine, commerce, and navigation" are called "the three civil arts," each having "a peculiar corporate privilege," which privilege is stated to be "by the grant and creation of the lord of the territory, authenticated by the judiciary, and distinct from the general privileges of a country and kindred."*

The great legislator is said to have flourished around the year 430 before Christ. At that time, then, assuming the clause in question to be authentic, the art of medicine was protected and encouraged by the state — a fact which, while it indicates some progress in medical knowledge, speaks well for the humanity and peaceful habits of the people in general.

Soon after the era usually assigned to Dyvnwal Moelmud — around 400 BC — Hippocrates lived, who is very generally regarded as the father of medicine, given that from his time medicine seems to have taken on the character of a science among the Greeks. Whether any of the British Ovates became acquainted with his system in the interval between that time and the Roman invasion, we are, of course, unable to say. It is possible that they might have gained some knowledge of his medical skill and treatment through the Phoceans, who traded between Marseilles and Britain; and we are certain that they were not men

* Ancient Laws and Institutions of Wales, Vol. ii. p. 515.

xii PREFACE.

to despise any opportunity that fell in their way of adding to the store of their general knowledge.

In later times, however, we find that Hippocrates was held in high esteem by the medical profession in this country, and the Physicians of Myddvai quote him with admiration.* But their familiarity with him was, no doubt, derived from a reading of his works, rather than through oral tradition.

There may be some people who are unwilling to accept the authority of our native records regarding the Druidic antiquity of the art of medicine among the Welsh. But there is not the slightest reason for any skepticism or doubt on the subject. On the contrary, the classical writers of Greece and Rome, as soon as they are able to speak to us on the matter, bear witness to a greater or lesser degree to the same fact, and support the general accuracy of our traditions. The physical researches of the Bards and Druids seem to have caught their particular attention. "The soothsayers," says Strabo, "are sacrificers and physiologists (φυσιολογοι.) The Druids in addition to physiology practise moral philosophy." Nature both external and human — causes and effects — diseases and their antidotes — all came within their knowledge, and in their hands underwent a thorough and practical investigation. Cicero informs us that he was personally acquainted with one of the Gallic Druids, Divitiacus the Aeduan, a man of standing in his country, who claimed to have a thorough knowledge of the laws of nature, including, as we may well suppose, the science of medicine.

* See § 176.

PREFACE. xiii

Pliny enumerates some of the plants most in repute among the Britons for their medicinal properties. He mentions the mistletoe, and observes that in Druidical language it signified "All heal," omnia sanantem — a name indicative of the efficacy which it was supposed to possess; and it is remarkable, as corroborative of his assertion, that Oll iach is to this very day one of the names by which the plant in question is known to the Cymry. Nor does it appear that its virtues, real or traditional, were forgotten in comparatively recent times. In the Book of Howel Veddyg, a descendant of the celebrated physicians of Myddvai, which forms the second part of the present volume, we are informed that the mistletoe was efficacious in cases of general debility — nervous complaints — brain fever — rheumatism — affection of the heart, liver, bowels, kidneys, spine — epilepsy — paralysis — insanity. It will strengthen the sight and hearing, and all the bodily senses — prevent barrenness — and "whosoever takes a spoonful of the powder in his ordinary drink once a day, shall have uninterrupted health, strength of body, and manly vigour."
Another plant mentioned by Pliny is the selago, a kind of club moss resembling savine, which, according to him, the Druids greatly admired for its medicinal qualities, particularly in diseases of the eyes.
The samolus, or marshwort, is said also to have been greatly used by them to cure their oxen and swine.
Welsh Botanology encompasses several plants which, either by name or tradition, are associated with the art of healing, and may be referred purely

* Lycopodium Selago, or Upright Fir Moss.
† Samolus Valerandi, or Water Pimpernel.

xiv PREFACE.

to Druidical times, or at least to times when the Bardic College enjoyed the protection of the state. Such are the Derwen Vendigaid, or Vervain, the symbol of Alban Hevin, as the Mistletoe was of Alban Arthan—Arian Cor—Arian Gwion—Berwr Taliesin—Bogail Gwener—Boled Olwen—Bronwen—Cerddinen—Clych Enid—Erbin—Eiriu Gwion—Ffaen Taliesin—Golch Enid—Llys y Dryw—Llys Taliesin—Meillionen Olwen—Pumbys yr Alban—Yspyddaden, with many others.

We do not know to what extent British medicine was influenced one way or other by Roman domination. It is very certain that the masters of the world did not generally regard our native institutions with a favorable eye; and since they themselves were not particularly celebrated in medicine, we are justified in supposing that the medical college gained no very great advantage from their rule. The Bards, however, though highly conservative, would not reject any genuine improvements which the Romans might bring to their attention, as we can infer from their behavior in other matters, such as their adoption of the Roman method of making parchment and books.

Soon after the departure of the Romans, a fondness for medical and physical pursuits once again became characteristic of our Cymric ancestors. The following constituents of man are attributed to the "Chief of Bards" in the 6th century.

"THE ELEMENTS OF MAN BY TALIESIN."

"Man consists of eight parts: the first is earth, which is sluggish and heavy, and from it comes the flesh. The second is stones, which are hard, and these are the materials of the bones. The third is water, which is moist and cold, and is the substance of the blood.

This page is already in English and requires no translation. The text describes the role, privileges, duties, and compensation of the Royal Court physician as recorded in the Laws of Hywel Dda. It outlines eighteen regulations governing the court mediciner, including his entitlements to land, clothing, lodging, and payment for various medical procedures, as well as his obligations to treat those in the palace without charge except in cases of the three gravest wounds. It further specifies compensation amounts for scarring injuries to the face, hand, and foot.

PREFACE. xvii

Every unexposed scar, four pence.
The cranium, four pence.*

For every broken bone, twenty pence; unless there be a dispute as to its size; and if there be a dispute as to the size, let the physician take a brass basin, and let him place his elbow upon the ground, and his hand over the basin, and if its sound be heard, let four legal pence be paid; and if it be not heard, nothing is due.

This singular test is made more clear in another place, as follows:

"Four small pennies are to be paid to a person for every bone taken from the upper part of the skull, which shall sound on falling into a copper basin."

If the physician was insulted while drunk he was not entitled to compensation, as "he knew not at what time the king might want his assistance."

He was "free to travel the road, and off the road—along with the messenger of the sick," and, as stated in legal fragments entitled "Elucidation," any one might take another's horse to procure a medical man for a person in danger without being required to make amends.

We have no reason to suppose that there was any material difference either in the position of the physicians, or in the attention paid to the study of medicine during the succeeding ages, until we come to the era of Rhys Gryg, when the Physicians of Myddvai flourished.

Rhys Gryg was the son of Rhys ab Gruffydd, prince of South Wales, and lived in the early part of the 13th century. He was a distinguished warrior, and fought with varied success in the wars which were carried on in Wales almost without interruption during his life. According to old custom he had his domestic

* Ancient Laws and Institutes of Wales, vol. I. p. 41, etc. † Ibid. p. 315. ‡ p. 507.
i.e. Rhys the Hoarse. This surname would seem to indicate that Rhys was afflicted with some disease of the larynx, or his hoarseness may have been the result of a wound in that part.

xviii PREFACE.

Physician, namely Rhiwallon, who was assisted by his three sons, Cadwgan, Gruffydd, and Einion, from a place called Myddvai, in the present county of Caermarthen, whose rights and privileges, as enjoined by law, were worthily maintained and upheld by the prince. Under his patronage these men made a collection of valuable medicinal recipes applicable to the various disorders to which the human body was then subject. But though this collection bears their name, we are not to suppose that all the prescriptions contained therein were the result of the studies and experience of the Physicians of Myddvai. Some no doubt had been in the materia medica of Wales long before; a few indeed may perhaps be traced back to the time of Howel the Good, if not to the sixth century. Such, however, do not seem to have been committed to writing until the Physicians of Myddvai took the matter in hand and produced the work, which is now printed for the first time. The original manuscript is supposed to be the one lately transferred from the library of the Welsh Charity School in London to the British Museum. Of this there are several copies; the one adopted as the basis of the present volume is from the Red Book in Jesus College, Oxford, which was carefully collated by the Rev. Robert Owen, B.D., Fellow of the said College, with a transcript made by the late Mr. Saunders from Mr. Rees of Tonn's copy; which manuscript was, moreover, copied around 1766 by William Bona of Llanpumsant, from another copy belonging to Iago ap Dewi of Llanllawddog. The various readings of the Tonn copy are all arranged at the foot of each page and referred to under the letter T.

PREFACE. xix

A knowledge of medicine was preserved in the descendants of this family, and they continued to practice as physicians at Myddvai, without intermission, until the middle of the last century.

The second portion of this volume purports to have been compiled by Howel the Physician, son of Rhys, son of Llewelyn, son of Philip the Physician, a lineal descendant of Einion, the son of Rhiwallon, from the Books of the first Physicians of Myddvai. William Bona made a transcript from the Book of John Jones, Physician of Myddvai, the last lineal descendant of the family, A.D. 1743. The late Iolo Morganwg took a copy of this MS. in 1801, and it is his copy, now in Llanover Library, that forms the text of our volume.

Besides these collections, several fragments, some indeed of considerable length, but of uncertain date, may be often met with in MSS. having for the most part, perhaps, been made by individual practitioners for their own private use, before the art of printing became general. Some medical prescriptions assumed a proverbial shape, and in that form clung firmly to the public mind. We subjoin a few of these; and as proverbs lose much of their point when translated, we give them first in their original form.

MEDICAL PROVERBS,
(From the Book of Iaco ab Dewi.)
He who sleeps without supper has no need of Rhiwallon of Myddvai.
A supper of apples, a breakfast of nuts.
A cool mouth and warm feet will make for a long life.
Go to the fish market in the morning, and to the meat market in the afternoon.
Cold water and warm bread make an unhealthy belly.
Water has three qualities: it brings neither sickness, debt, nor widowhood.
Eating eggs without salt causes illness.
It is no insult to take an old man's supper from him.
Eel in a pastry, and lamprey in salt.

xx PREFACE.

A fever or ague at the fall of the leaf is always long or fatal.
Want in a month, a lamb in three months.
Dry feet, fresh mouth.
A grayling and a Lenten sermon.
A night meal has killed more than the Physicians of Myddvai ever cured.
A light supper, a lighter night meal, good sleep, long life.
Do not be greedy for milk after fish.
Much sleep is the health of youth and the sickness of old age.
Long youth shortens life.
It is healthier to smell warm food than to eat it.
A short illness to the body and a short frost to the earth cure and strengthen; but either prolonged destroys.
While the urine is clear, let the physician go beg.
Appetite is better than gluttony.
Plenty of bread, little drink.
Yesterday's bread, today's meat, and last year's wine make for good health.
Quench your thirst where the washerwoman fetches her water.
Three men shall be long-lived: the dryland ploughman, the mountain shepherd, and the sea fisherman.
Three feasts of health: milk, bread, and salt.
The three remedies of the Physicians of Myddvai: water, honey, and labour.
Health is moderate labour.
Three moderations that make long life: diet, labour, and meditation.
He who breaks his fast in May, let him count himself among the dead.
Whoever sees fennel and does not gather it is no man but a devil.
If you wish to die, eat cabbage broth in August.
However much you eat, drink three times.
God sends food to washed hands.
Drink water like an ox, and wine like a king.
One egg is thrift, two is gentility, three is boldness, and the fourth is excess.
If people knew how good a hen is in January, not one would be left on the roost.
Sheep's cheese, goat's milk, cow's butter are the best.
Three healthful relishes: honey, butter, and milk.
Three unhealthful relishes: meat, ale, and vinegar.
Do not take off your vest before Ascension Day.
If you wish to fall ill, wash your head and go to sleep.
There is no goodness or nourishment in broth without herbs.
If you wish to die, eat roast mutton and sleep soon after.
If you have eaten something bad, eat roast hare.
Mustard after food.
He who cleans his teeth with the point of his knife may soon be cleaning them with the handle.
A dry cough is the trumpet of death.

MEDICAL MAXIMS,
(From the Book of Iago ab Dewi.)

He who goes to sleep without supper will have no need of Rhiwallon of Myddvai.

Apples for supper, nuts for breakfast.

A cold mouth and warm feet will lead to a long life.

Go to the fish market in the morning, and to the butcher's shop in the afternoon.

Cold water and warm bread will upset the stomach.

Water has three qualities: it causes no sickness, no debt, and no widowhood.

Eating eggs without salt will make you ill.

It is no offense to deny an old man his supper.

Eel in a pie, lampreys in salt.

A fever or ague that comes in autumn always lasts a long time, or else proves fatal.

A kid should be one month old before eating, a lamb three months.

Keep your feet dry and your tongue moist.

Salmon and a sermon belong to Lent.

Overeating at supper will kill more people than all the Physicians of Myddvai ever cured.

Eat lightly at dinner, less at supper, sleep soundly, and live long.

Do not drink milk after eating fish.

Sleeping a lot is good for the young, but harmful for the old.

Good health enjoyed too long in youth shortens one's life.

It is healthier to smell warm bread than to eat it.

A short illness for the body, and a brief frost for the earth, will both do good; prolonged, either one will destroy.

While a patient's urine is clear, the physician may as well beg for work.

Appetite is better than gluttony.

Eat enough bread, but drink little.

Yesterday's bread, today's meat, and last year's wine will keep you healthy.

Quench your thirst where the washerwoman draws her water.

Three types of men tend to live long: the ploughman of dry land, the mountain dairyman, and the fisherman of the sea.

The three foods of health are milk, bread, and salt.

The three medicines of the Physicians of Myddvai are water, honey, and hard work.

Moderate exercise is the foundation of health.

Three things in moderation will lead to a long life: food, work, and reflection.

Whoever does not break their fast in May should consider themselves as good as dead.

A man who sees fennel and does not pick it is no man at all, but a devil.

If you wish to die, eat cabbage in August.

The Legend of Llyn-y-Fan-Fach,
or
The Lady of the Lake.

THE

LEGEND OF LLYN-Y-VAN-VACH,

OR THE ORIGIN OF

The Physicians of Myddfai,

COLLECTED FROM VARIOUS SOURCES, IN THE YEAR 1841.

When the eventful struggle made by the Princes of South Wales to preserve the independence of their country was drawing to its close in the twelfth century, there lived at Blaensawdde, near Llanddeusant, Carmarthenshire, a widowed woman, the relict of a farmer who had fallen in those disastrous troubles.

The widow had an only son to bring up, and Providence smiled upon her, and, despite her forlorn condition, her livestock had so increased over time that she could not well pasture them upon her farm, so she sent a portion of her cattle to graze on the adjoining Black Mountain, and their most favourite place was near the small lake called Llyn-y-Van-Vach, on the North Western side of the Carmarthenshire Vans.

xxii LEGEND OF LLYN-Y-VAN,

The son grew up to manhood, and was generally sent by his mother to look after the cattle on the mountain. One day, while wandering along the margin of the lake, to his great astonishment he beheld, sitting on the calm surface of the water, a Lady — one of the most beautiful creatures that mortal eyes had ever seen. Her hair flowed gracefully in ringlets over her shoulders, and she arranged her tresses with a comb, using the glassy surface of her watery resting place as a mirror to reflect her own image. Suddenly she noticed the young man standing at the edge of the lake, his eyes fixed upon her, unconsciously holding out to her the barley bread and cheese he had been given when he left home.

Overcome by feelings of love and admiration for the vision before him, he continued to hold out his hand toward the lady, who glided imperceptibly closer to him, but gently refused his offering of food. He attempted to touch her, but she slipped from his grasp, saying:

"Your bread is hard-baked!
I am not easy to catch."

And immediately she dived beneath the water and disappeared, leaving the lovesick youth to return home consumed by disappointment and regret that he had been unable to become better acquainted with someone beside whom all the fair maidens of Llanddeusant and Myddvai he had ever seen amounted to nothing.

*Myddvai parish was, in former times, celebrated for its beautiful maidens, but whether they were descendants of the Lady of the Lake or not cannot be determined. An old pennill records their beauty thus:

There is white snow
On the mountain's brow,
And greenwood at the Verdre,
Young birch so good
In Cwm-brân wood,
And lovely girls in Myddve.

On his return home the young man told his mother about the extraordinary vision he had witnessed. She advised him to carry some unbaked dough, or "toes," in his pocket next time, as there must have been some enchantment connected with the hard-baked bread, or "Bara cras," that had prevented him from catching the lady.

The next morning, before the sun had touched the peaks of the Vans with its rays, the young man was already at the lake — not to tend his mother's cattle, but to seek again the enchanting vision he had seen the day before. But it was all in vain; he anxiously strained his eyes and searched the surface of the lake, finding only ripples stirred up by a stiff breeze, while a cloud hung heavily over the summit of the Van, adding to the gloom that already weighed on his troubled mind.

Hours passed. The wind grew still, and the clouds that had wrapped the mountain dissolved into thin air before the powerful rays of the sun, when the youth was suddenly startled to see some of his mother's cattle on the steep slope on the far side of the lake. Duty compelled him to try to rescue them from their dangerous position, and as he hastened off to do so, the object of his search appeared to him again, just as before, and seemed even more beautiful than when he had first seen her. He held out his hand to her again, filled with unbaked bread, and offered it along with an earnest declaration of his heart and vows of eternal devotion — all of which she refused, saying:

"Llaith dy fara!
Ti ni fynna'."

Unbaked is thy bread!
I will not have thee.

Yet the smiles that played across her face as the lady disappeared beneath the waters gave the young man a hope that kept him from despair at her refusal, and the memory of those smiles cheered him on his way home. He told his aged mother of his failure, and she suggested that he should next time bring bread that was only lightly baked, as that would most likely please the mysterious being with whom he had fallen in love.

Driven by an irresistible feeling, the youth left his mother's house early the next morning and made his way swiftly over the

mountain. He was soon near the edge of the lake, and with all the impatience of an eager lover, he waited with feverish anxiety for the mysterious lady to reappear.

The sheep and goats grazed on the steep sides of the Van; the cattle wandered among the rocks and large stones, some of which were occasionally dislodged from their places and suddenly rolled down into the lake. Rain and sunshine alike came and went, but the youth paid attention to none of it, so wholly absorbed was he in watching for the lady to appear.

The freshness of the early morning had given way before the sultry rays of the midday sun, which in its turn was rapidly moving westward as evening faded and made way for the darkness of night. Hope of seeing the Lady of the Lake once more had nearly died away. The young man cast a sad and final farewell look across the waters, and to his astonishment saw several cows walking along its surface. The sight of these animals revived his hope that something far more pleasing would follow them, and he was not disappointed, for the maiden reappeared, looking to his enraptured eyes even lovelier than before. She came toward the shore, and he rushed into the water to meet her. A smile from her encouraged him to take her hand; she did not refuse the moderately baked bread he offered her; and after some persuasion she agreed to become his bride, on the condition that they should only live together until she received from him three blows without cause —

"Tri ergyd diachos."

Three causeless blows.

— and if he should ever strike her three such blows, she would leave him forever. To these conditions he readily agreed, and would have agreed to any other terms had they been proposed, since he was only intent on securing such a lovely creature as his wife.

So the lady of the lake agreed to become the young man's wife, and having freed her hand for a moment, she darted away and dived into the lake. His disappointment and grief were such that he resolved to throw himself headlong into the deepest water, so as to end his life in the very element that held in its unfathomable depths the only one for whom he wished to live on earth. As he was on the point of carrying out this rash act, there emerged out

OR THE LADY OF THE LAKE. XXV

of the lake two most beautiful ladies accompanied by a white-haired man of noble bearing and extraordinary stature, yet possessing all the vigor and strength of youth. This man addressed the nearly bewildered young man in tones designed to calm his troubled mind, saying that since he wished to marry one of his daughters, he would consent to the union — provided the young man could identify which of the two ladies before him was the one he loved. This was no easy task, as the maidens were such perfect mirror images of each other that it seemed quite impossible for him to choose his bride, and if by chance he chose the wrong one, all would be lost forever.

While the young man carefully studied the two ladies, he could detect no difference whatsoever between them, and was nearly giving up in despair, when one of them pushed her foot slightly forward. The movement, simple as it was, did not escape the young man's notice, and he spotted a small difference in the way their sandals were tied. This immediately resolved the dilemma, for he had on previous occasions been so struck by the Lady of the Lake's overall appearance that he had also noticed the beauty of her feet and ankles, and now, recognizing the distinctive way her shoe was tied, he boldly took hold of her hand.

"You have chosen correctly," said her father. "Be a kind and faithful husband to her, and I will give her, as a dowry, as many sheep, cattle, goats, and horses as she can count of each kind, without taking a breath. But remember: if you are ever unkind to her and strike her three times without cause, she shall return to me and take all her livestock with her."

Such was the verbal marriage agreement, to which the young man gladly consented. His bride was then asked to count the number of sheep she was to receive. She immediately began counting in fives — one, two, three, four, five; one, two, three, four, five — as many times as possible in rapid succession, until her breath gave out. The same method of counting was used to determine the number of goats, cattle, and horses respectively, and in an instant the full number of each came out of the lake when summoned by the Father.

The young couple were then married, though by what ceremony was not recorded, and afterwards went to live at a farm called Esgair

xxvi LEGEND OF LLYN Y VAN,

Llaethdy, somewhat more than a mile from the village of Myddvai, where they lived in prosperity and happiness for several years, and became the parents of three sons, who were beautiful children.

Once upon a time there was a christening to take place in the neighbourhood, to which the parents were specially invited. When the day arrived the wife appeared very reluctant to attend the christening, claiming that the distance was too great for her to walk. Her husband told her to fetch one of the horses which were grazing in an adjoining field. "I will," said she, "if you will bring me my gloves which I left in our house." He went to the house and returned with the gloves, and finding that she had not gone for the horse, he jokingly slapped her shoulder with one of them, saying "go! go!" (dos, dos). She then reminded him of the agreement upon which she had consented to marry him — that he was not to strike her without cause — and warned him to be more cautious in the future.

On another occasion when they were together at a wedding, in the midst of the merriment and high spirits of the assembled guests who had gathered from all the surrounding country, she burst into tears and sobbed most piteously. Her husband touched her on her shoulder and asked the reason for her weeping. She said "now people are entering into trouble, and your troubles are likely to begin, as you have now struck me a second time without cause."

Years passed, and their children had grown up and were particularly clever young men. In the midst of so many worldly blessings at home, the husband almost forgot that there remained only one causeless blow left to be given that would destroy the whole of his prosperity. Still he was watchful lest any trivial occurrence should take place which his wife might regard as a breach of their marriage contract. She told him, as her affection for him remained strong, to be careful that he would not through some carelessness give the last and only blow which, by an unalterable destiny over which she had no control, would separate them forever.

It so happened, however, that one day they were together at a funeral, where, in the midst of the mourning and grief at the house of the deceased, she appeared in the highest and most cheerful spirits, and broke into uncontrollable fits of laughter, which so shocked her husband that he touched her, saying "Hush! Hush! Don't laugh." She said that she laughed "because people when

OR THE LADY OF THE LAKE. xxvii

they die go out of trouble," and, rising up, she went out of the house, saying, "The last blow has been struck, our marriage contract is broken, and at an end! Farewell!" Then she started off towards Esgair Llaethdy, where she called her cattle and other stock together, each by name. The cattle she called thus:—

"Brindled cow, white speckled,
Spotted cow, bold freckled,
The four field sward mottled,
The old white-faced,
And the grey Geingen,
With the white Bull,
From the court of the King;
And the little black calf
Though suspended on the hook,
Come you also, quite well home!"

They all immediately obeyed the summons of their mistress; the "little black calf," although it had been slaughtered, came back to life and walked off with the rest of the stock at the command of the Lady. This happened in the spring of the year, and there were four oxen ploughing in one of the fields; to these she cried,

"The four grey oxen,
That are on the field,
Come you also,
Quite well home!"

The whole of the livestock went away with the Lady across Myddvai Mountain, towards the lake from which they had come, a distance of over six miles, where they disappeared beneath its waters, leaving no trace behind except a well-marked furrow, which was made by the plough the oxen drew after them into the lake, and which remains to this day as proof of the truth of this story.

xxviii LEGEND OF LLYN-Y-VAN,

What became of the frightened ploughman — whether he was left in the field when the oxen set off, or whether he followed them to the lake — has not been preserved by tradition; nor has the fate of the heartbroken and half-ruined husband been kept in memory. But of the sons it is recorded that they often wandered about the lake and its surroundings, hoping that their mother might be allowed to visit the surface of the earth once more, for they had been told of her mysterious origin, her first appearance to their father, and the unfortunate circumstances that so unhappily deprived them of her maternal care.

On one of their walks, at a place near Dôl Howel, at the Mountain Gate, still called "Llidiad y Meddygon" — the Physicians' Gate — the mother appeared suddenly and approached her eldest son, whose name was Rhiwallon, and told him that his purpose on earth was to be a benefactor to humanity by relieving people from pain and misery through healing all manner of their diseases. For this purpose she provided him with a bag full of medical prescriptions and instructions for preserving health, saying that through careful attention to these, he and his family would become for many generations the most skilled physicians in the land. Then, promising to meet him when her guidance was most needed, she vanished. But on several occasions she met her sons near the shores of the lake, and once she even accompanied them on their way home as far as a place still called "Pant-y-Meddygon" — the Physicians' Dingle — where she pointed out to them the various plants and herbs growing there and revealed their medicinal qualities and virtues. The knowledge she shared with them, combined with their unrivalled skill, soon brought them a fame that no one had ever achieved before. And so that their knowledge would not be lost, they wisely committed it to writing for the benefit of all humanity through all ages.

And so ends the story of the Physicians of Myddvai, which has been passed down from one generation to another, thus:

"The grey old man in the corner
heard a tale from his father,
and his father had heard it from his father before him,
and after them I have kept it in memory."

OR THE LADY OF THE LAKE. xxix

As stated in the Introduction of the present Work, Rhiwallon and his sons became Physicians to Rhys Gryg, Lord of Llandovery and Dynevor Castles, "who gave them rank, lands, and privileges at Myddvai for their maintenance in the practice of their art and science, and the healing and benefit of those who should seek their help," thus affording to those who could not afford to pay, the best medical advice and treatment, free of charge. Such a truly Royal Foundation could not fail to produce corresponding effects. So the fame of the Physicians of Myddvai was soon established throughout the whole country, and continued for centuries among their descendants.

The celebrated Welsh Bard, Dafydd ap Gwilym, who flourished in the following century, and was buried at the Abbey of Tal-y-llychau, in Carmarthenshire, around the year 1368, says in one of his Poems, as quoted in Dr. Davies' Dictionary:

"He would not make a physician in the manner that Myddvai made, if he had a man raised on mead."

A Physician he would not make
As Myddvai made, if he had a mead-fostered man.

Of the lands bestowed upon the Physicians, there are two farms in Myddvai parish still called "Llwyn Ifan Feddyg," the Grove of Evan the Physician, and "Llwyn Meredydd Feddyg," the Grove of Meredith the Physician. Esgaer Llaethdy, mentioned in the foregoing Legend, was formerly in the possession of the above descendants, as was Ty newydd, near Myddvai, which was purchased by Mr. Holford, of Cilgwyn, from the Rev. Charles Lloyd, Vicar of Llandefalle, Breconshire, who married a daughter of one of the Physicians, and received the living of Llandefalle from a Mr. Vaughan, who gave it to him out of gratitude, because Mr. Lloyd's wife's father had cured him of a disease of the eye. As Mr. Lloyd came into that living in 1748 and died in 1800, it is probable that the skilled eye doctor was John Jones, who is mentioned in the following inscription on a tombstone currently fixed against the west end of Myddvai Church.

HERE
Lies the body of Mr. David Jones, of Mothvey, Surgeon,
who was an honest, charitable, and skillful man.
He died September 14th, Anno Domini 1719, aged 61.

JOHN JONES, Surgeon,
Eldest son of the said David Jones, departed this life
the 25th of November, 1789, in the 44th year
of his Age, and is also interred hereunder.

xxx THE LEGEND OF LLYN-Y-VAN.

These appear to have been the last of the Physicians who practised at Myddvai. The above John Jones resided for some time at Llandovery, and was a very eminent surgeon. One of his descendants named John Lewis lived at Cwmbran, Myddvai, at which place his great grandson Mr. John Jones now resides.

Dr. Morgan Owen, Bishop of Llandaff, who died at Glasallt, parish of Myddvai, in 1645, was a descendant of the Meddygon, and an inheritor of much of their landed property in that parish, the bulk of which he bequeathed to his nephew, Morgan Owen, who died in 1667, and was succeeded by his son, Henry Owen; and at the death of the last of whose descendants, Robert Lewis, Esq., the estates passed through the will of one of the family to the late D. A. S. Davies, Esq., M.P. for Caermarthenshire.

Bishop Owen bequeathed to another nephew, Morgan ap Rees, son of Rees ap John, a descendant of the Meddygon, the farm of Rhyblid and some other property. Morgan ap Rees's son, Samuel Rice, resided at Loughor in Gower, Glamorganshire, and had a son, Morgan Rice, who was a merchant in London and became Lord of the Manor of Tooting Graveney, and High Sheriff in the year 1772, and Deputy Lieutenant of the County of Surrey in 1776. He resided at Hill House, which he built. At his death the whole of his property passed to his only child, John Rice, Esq., whose eldest son, the Rev. John Morgan Rice, inherited the greater portion of his estates. The head of the family is now the Rev. Horatio Morgan Rice, Rector of South Hill with Callington, Cornwall, and Justice of the Peace for the County, who inherited, along with other property, a small estate at Loughor. The above Morgan Rice had landed property in Llanmadock and Llangenith, as well as Loughor, in Gower, but whether he had any connection with Howel the Physician (ap Rhys ap Llywelyn ap Philip the Physician, and lineal descendant from Einion ap Rhiwallon), who resided at Cilgwryd in Gower, is not known.

Among other families who claim descent from the Physicians were the Bowens of Cwmydw, Myddvai, and the Joneses of Dollgarreg and Penrhock in the same parish, the latter of whom are represented by Charles Bishop of Dollgareg, Esq., Clerk of the Peace for Caermarthenshire, and Thomas Bishop of Brecon, Esq.

Rees Williams of Myddvai is recorded as one of the Meddygon. His great grandson was the late Rice Williams, M.D. of Aberystwyth, who died May 16th, 1842, aged 85, and appears to have been the last, though not the least eminent, of the Physicians descended from the mysterious Lady of Llyn-y-Van.

The Physicians of Myddfai.

§ 1. Here, with the support of the most high God, are set forth the most distinguished and foremost medical remedies for the human body; and it was Rhiwallon the physician and his sons — namely, Cadwgan, Gruffudd, and Einion — who caused them to be written down in this manner. For they were the best and foremost of the physicians of their time; and in the time of Rhys Gryg, their lord, and lord of Dinefwr, he was the man¹ who maintained their privilege and their due in full toward them, honorably as was fitting.

And the reason they caused their skills to be written down in this manner was lest there should be anyone who knew as much as they, after them.

§ 2. And of the foremost and first things that God formed of the human body: the head is that thing, for in it are the five senses of the body.

§ 3. Three places in the head where diseases are bred: one is the scalp; the second is the temple; the third is the brain.

2 THE PHYSICIANS OF MYDDVAI.

§ 4. If one opens [a wound] on the head as far as the skull, and the venom flows away, the skull is preserved. With blood and burnings the surface is preserved.

§ 5. If one opens [a wound] on the creature and then takes two parts of the bark of the herb and one part of violet; and salted butter; and beats them together, and applies it to it. This will draw out the venom of the wound. If inflammation and venom arise in it.

§ 6. If the wound is opened on the surface until, by the ninth day, there is proud flesh on the bone: this is caused by an old disease of the head.

§ 7. If there is a fresh bruise or a fresh contusion on the head, the best thing is to drain it first, to prevent blood from falling on the wound and festering there. If the bone is laid bare on the wound; take violet and fresh butter and beat them together; and if violet cannot be had, take white of egg and linen, and beat them together; or fresh butter and linen; and apply it to the wound in the evening, and then make an ointment of herbs and butter and wax and apply it until it is healed. A pound is the fee of the physician for that treatment in charity without maintenance; or nine score with maintenance.

§ 8. For a pain in the eye: burn in the hollow of the eyebrow and another at the nape of the neck: this is good against the moisture of the head.

§ 9. For red eyes, inflamed, place a leech under the two eyes, and burn at the nape of the neck. This is good against moisture of the head.

§ 10. For dry scab: take the juice of elder, and lard of a hen, and honey-butter and beat them together, and put them in a horn: and when you go to sleep, anoint your eyes and your eyelids well, and they will be healed.

§ 11. There are three kinds of lungs: dry lungs, and white lungs; and a pain under the two breasts, and under the arm. And

PHYSICIANS OF MYDDVAI. 3

the top of the shoulder, and reddening of the cheeks. And thus the physician shall proceed: take three days of herb-broth from these herbs; for the joints, for the red foot, and for the ailment of the intestines. And then three more days; for the diaphragm. And after the disease has been drawn out from its seat, raise the man up by the end of the fourth day. And then prepare a medicinal drink through ground wheat, or through red wine, with these herbs: for the wormwood, for the boar's wort, for the fleabane, and for the liverwort, and for the eye of the day, and for the broad plantain, and for erchwreid; and the roots of the whitebeam, and heather, and hazel, and ground-ivy, and heather-stalks, and the blessed houseleek, and cleavers; and whatever herbs the physician wills besides. In this manner the white poultice is made: take May butter, and goat's tallow, or deer's grease, and knitbone, and whatever herbs one wills for that purpose. A lung-wound is the third degree of a physician's concern: for the physician cannot set a limit to it; but only await the will of God. Through the following herbs a medicinal drink is made for one who has a lung-wound upon him, to drain and sustain as a lung-wound ought, in its temperature. And within eleven years, death from it is most common.

§ 12. There are four fevers which arise from the nature of summer; namely, a slow fever, and a shivering fever, and a sudden-death fever, and a hot fever; and the fifth fever is a fever of the head; and from the root of that one, the slow fever. A slow fever is cured by raising a liquid and a burning. Here is its nature: from generating too much moisture in the stomach; and thereby a loathing of food and weakening through the summer. The grey roots, and the glasswort, and the echwreid, and the vilftyth, and hemp, and red cabbage, and turch, and the seven herbs that correspond to each one of those: Whoever might obtain them together, his sickness would not long endure.

4 THE PHYSICIANS OF MYDDVAI.

against a bite of the lungs through which life might pass. And these are the herbs for that: liverwort, elder, blessed herb, smooth herb, red-rooted herb, and wall pennywort, broad-leafed plantain, blue-topped herb, pellitory, eye of the day, hard-head, and the root of red nettle, the heathers, and sloe, and tooth-wort, and the root of the briar, and heather, and hazel, and the herb that keeps one alive, and ground-elder, and the bee's herb of the river, and small cudweed, and moneywort along with them.

§ 13. For a shivering fever: take the tooth of a garlic and the steam of the earth and pour them on the water of morning, and drink first, and at midday take wormwood and pour it on water and drink until the tenth part, and cease then from drinking; and take a loaf of wheaten bread or oaten bread, and goat's mead, and chicken broth, and the pressing of water through cloth, and abstain from milk and all that is made of milk. And if the fever does not cease, put the person in an ointment at the hour the fever comes upon him, and give him rest in the ointment according to its strength.

§ 14. The best three drinks to break a fever: apple drink, and goat's mead, and spring water.

§ 15. Another medicine against shivering fever: take the grey root, the great herb of grace, the blessed herb of grace, the red-rooted herb, the dwarf elder, the gullet-wort, and the bark of the elder, and horehound; and boil them together in a pot or cauldron as well as can be done. And then take the water and the herbs and put them in the ointment. These are the kinds of medicine that are good for that: take the moss and the spreading root, or the bark of the horse, and if not obtained, brooklime; and boil those two herbs well. And then take the horehound and the fennel, and the dwarf elder, and the gullet-wort, and the glasswort, and the herb that keeps alive, and press them as well as can be done; and put them on the fire together with the two herbs previously mentioned, and boil them well. And then take the

PHYSICIANS OF MYDDVAI. 5

the bark that grows on the elder tree; and grate and wash it well, and pound it in a mortar thoroughly; and then take the liquid thereof upon the herbs aforesaid, and pour the said liquid over the said herbs between two hands in a straining manner, and put it into a vessel to settle; and rack it off with the dregs of beer; or ox-gall. And drink a good draught of this each morning for as long as it lasts: and then take a little honey, or an apple, or berries, to take away the taste from the lips. That liquid is good for every person who wishes to purify his body.

§ 16. There are two kinds of letywigwst: moist letywigwst, and dry letywigwst, from the heat of summer when it ceases. Moist letywigwst from the dampness of summer at that time; and the treatment is to open the two veins that come from the liver opposite each other: and thus it is cured: bind the three of them above; and leave the fourth one free; and apply burnings upon the shin-bones, and around the sinews, and the joints. And let the blood of the fundament, and the joints; and after all the burnings have been performed by the vein. The second treatment for this is: take hops and boil them in strong wheat-ale, or spring water; and then take the bark of the elder-tree, and pound it well in a mortar, and strain it upon that liquid, and give the patient to drink, to purify his system. And thereafter forbid him beef, and cheese, and leeks, and large fish and salmon, and eels, and wildfowl, and garlic, and all dairy foods; except the whey of warm milk.

§ 17. There are four kinds of bolwyst: bolwyst of the fluid, bolwyst of the system, bolwyst of the bladder, and bolwyst of the wind. Bolwyst of the fluid cannot be cured; bolwyst of the wind likewise has no remedy. It is not immediately fatal. Bolwyst of the system comes from bile, and it is cured by glasgyfleith and medicinal herbs. These are the herbs for those. The

6 THE PHYSICIANS OF MYDDVAI.

urine, the nipple, the armpit, the groin, the glands, the groin-gland, the underpits, the running sore, and the swellings of the armpits and the hocks. And this is how this swelling is treated: take the mucus and bury it in its navel; wash it well, and dry it gently; and pound it in a mortar as well as possible; and strain it through a cloth. And then put that liquid in a pan on the fire, and then take the decoction until it turns white, and keep it with you as long as you may; and make it into small pills when you give it to the patient. Swellings of burns, eruptions, and boils are cured by this.

§ 18. There are two kinds of warts that come to sit upon a person, and this is how they are cured: cut them with cold iron; and burn their place, and anoint them with honey.

§ 19. There are three kinds of hardness: dry hardness; from a swelling and liquid, and burns that dry out, these are cured. A stone that is hard like this is cured where it causes pain: take a rod and put it bent within the joint. And then put two pieces of skin from within the joint, and bend them upward around the rod; and bind a bandage around the two wrists, and around the neck, and lay it with its back upward. And if it is a high thing between the two thighs: from the left side push the pipe of the stone. And then put it in a water ointment that same day, and the next day first in a water ointment, and after that in a poultice. And after that put it in bed with its back upward: and dry the wound, and put linen and salted butter upon it, and maintain it in that condition until the skin grows together, changing the dressing morning and night before treating it; without food and without drink; and put it in the ointment. If there be gravel-stone; make a medicine through strong, clear, firm wheat with these herbs: cleavers, blessed spurge, orchwreid, erinllys, and ivy

PHYSICIANS OF MYDDVAI. 7

earth, and tansy and elecampane, and columbine, and motherwort, and dodder, and crampweed, and danhogen, and glessyn, and lion's tooth, and white cinquefoil, and red-topped herb, and brooklime.

§ 20. A woman who has difficulty in conceiving: through these herbs a remedy is made for her: the hedgehog herb and the right amount of tansy, and red-topped herb, and yellow herb, and the bull's herb, and the gan-wein, and diwythyl; and mixing all of these together, let her take a rising from it.

§ 21. A woman who is afflicted with the women's disease to excess: take fine mugwort, and fine bog-moss, and ganywein, and roec, and diwythyl, and hazel-shoots, and ash-bark as much as may cover her horns upon her head, and boil them in the best red wine that may be had: and strain that liquid well and drink it daily for as long as it takes, and refrain from the rich foods mentioned above and from excessive bloodletting at the veins and tendons.

§ 22. The root of the hiccup herb to break the hiccups; strike it upon cold water and drink it, and hold that in the mouth.

§ 23. Lion's tooth to raise the skull-bone of an old person — strike it upon cold water and drink it.

§ 24. Garlic of the snakes upon a scar; the juice of the root of tormentil to break; and the juice of their leaves to break a rupture.

§ 25. The roots of white cinquefoil, boil them, through wine to break a hernia also, and make through their leaves to kill worms.

§ 26. The roots of the feverfew and the roots of the elder, and the herbs of cadwgawn, and butter, and old lard, and brimstone — cast them together and press them through linen; that is good against the scab.

§ 27. From the time a cow calves until the end of the fifteenth day, her milk will be thick. And from then until the time she is put to the bull while she is in milk, her milk will be thick. Pig's flesh of a year old, and mutton, will be watery; and a man who has a watery complaint from disease — that meat is not good for him.

§ 28. The best meat of wild four-footed animals is venison. The best meat of tame four-footed animals is pork. The best meat of wild birds is partridge. The best meat of tame birds is hen. The best sea fish is flounder. The best freshwater fish are roach and trout.

§ 29. For a wet scurf-sore: the gall of a woodpecker, and marrow of a deer, and storax gum.

§ 30. For toothache: take the bark of the nearest elder tree, and the leaves of the woodbine, and pound them together in a mortar thoroughly, and squeeze them through a linen cloth into two vessels, and that will cure the complaint.

§ 31. For deafness: take the trunk of an elder tree, and the juice of ash berries, and squeeze them into the ear, and also under the teeth; and put a burnt piece of elder pith into the ear; and bind the jaw; and a walnut applied thus is good.

§ 32. For the bite of a snake: if it be a man, take a living cockerel and apply its vent to the bite, and hold it thus, and this is good. If it be a woman, take a living hen in the same manner, and that will draw out the poison.

§ 33. For a crab louse: take garlic and barley meal and red wine, and boil them together into a porridge, and apply it. And that is the remedy in a place that will not dry out.

§ 34. For pain in the head, or for a headache: take a wheaten loaf of the third baking, and grind it into fine flour, and then take wood sorrel, and the leaves of the burdock, and the bark of the elder, and red wine, and pound the herbs together in a mortar thoroughly, and mix them together on the fire, and nearly to the consistency of gruel, adding beef fat and salt. And then apply this plaster to the head after shaving it; and this is upon the authority that it will cause boils to break out on the third day, and draw out the poison from the extremities, and relieve the pain.

PHYSICIANS OF MYDDVAI. 9

§ 35. An adder's bite will not be poisonous from the Feast of the Virgin in harvest time until the Feast of the Virgin of the Candles; and during that time the adder's fangs will not be venomous, and this renders them harmless.

§ 36. For intestinal worms: take the bark of the elder, the bark of the French hazel, and the bark of the dwarf elder at the elbow joint; and boil them together in water, and drink a bowlful daily on an empty stomach, and refrain from food until midday; and continue this until the end of nine meals.

§ 37. For the bite of a toad: take yellow watercress and apply it to the wound, and it will heal quickly.

§ 38. For a wound: take the herb agrimony, and apply it to the wound as soon as it is found. Another way: take the flowers of the hard-head, or the leaves, bruise them together with the yolk of an egg and fine salt, and apply to the wound; and this will heal it. Another way: take the green chickweed, bruise it together with old lard, and apply to the wound. Another way: take the roots of the red nettle and the roots of the grey-blue grass, at their stalks; boil them together in the strained juice of goat's whey, thickened; and put butter in the liquid, and drink it night and day.

§ 39. For a wound after the pieces have broken off, or for a sore: take the eyelash plant, grind it well, sift it, and anoint the wound with it fresh; and sprinkle the flour of the herbs upon it; and this will make the wound good and fair. It is proper to boil all salves in strained milk.

§ 40. To stop a running flow of blood: take the plantain and strike it against cold water; and drink it, and this will stop it by the power of God.

§ 41. For a cough: take the hazel catkin and the agrimony; and boil them in pure milk; and put butter into it over the fire; and boil a good broth together, and drink it every morning.

§ 42. For toothache: take the blue henbane, and place it under the jaw wrapped in a fresh linen cloth, and it will heal. Another way: take—

10 PHYSICIANS OF MYDDVAI.

ready, the green remedy. And to place it in a tablet under the teeth; or on a warm stone, and place it warm inside linen under the aching tooth. Another is to take plantain, and bruise it well, and apply it to the aching tooth overnight. Another is to take the white dead-nettle, and beat it into a paste.

§ 43. For disease of the breast: take the old broad-leafed plantain and fat, and apply it, and it will heal.

§ 44. For worms: take wine and wormwood, and mix them together, and drink every morning on an empty stomach.

§ 45. For a snake-bite: take plantain, hard-head, and blue-head, and beat them into water and drink it. There are three injuries that a physician must treat: a wound to the lungs, a bruise of the chest, and a wound to the knee.

§ 46. For horse-pox: take white storax and soften it; and apply it gently, and this will heal it.

§ 47. There are seven enemies of the eyes: weeping, and crying, and watching, and drunkenness, and fornication, and dry-eye, and smoke.

§ 48. There are three bones in a man which, if they break, never knit again; and no man is born without them when he is born: the teeth, the kneecap, and the jaw.

§ 49. Bruise the grains of the poppy in wine to cause a man to sleep soundly.

§ 50. To prevent hiccups: take meadowsweet, and beat it into water and drink it at once.

§ 51. For a fever: take the grey herb-bennet, red nettle, and plantain, and bruise them well in old whey and boil them; and let the patient drink a cupful every morning, and this will make him well.

§ 52. For toothache: take a tallow candle made from sheep's fat (and sea-holly berries together with the fat) and burn the candle

PHYSICIANS OF MYDDVAI. 11

so that one may place the teeth and put cold water beneath the candle: and the worms will fall down into the water away from the heat of the candle.

§ 53. For a worm in a man's womb [belly]: take sheep's butter and oat flour, and the leaves of the brooklime herb, and the stalk in the fresh wind, and apply this to it: and if there be a scab upon it, it will heal.

For a worm in a man's belly also: take the urine of a he-goat on its own, and rub the scraping of the he-goat's horn upon it, and drink it for three days, and the worm will depart.

§ 54. For the falling sickness: burn a goat's horn and blow the smoke upon the man's head, and through the smell of it he will recover in that place; and before the man rises from there place a dog's bristle on his head: and that sickness will never come upon him again after that.

§ 55. For every tertian fever, write within three apples on three successive days: in the first apple ✠ o naglapater. In the second apple ✠ o nagla filius. In the third apple ✠ o vagla spiritus sanctus. By the third day he will be well. If you wish to know whether the sick man will live or die from his illness, take the herb called the dock and tie a strand about his two wrists, and if the sick man sleeps where he lies, he will recover, and if he cannot sleep he will die.

56. If you wish not to be drunk: drink in the morning a shell-full of the juice of bitter wormwood. If you wish not to be weary from walking, drink in the morning a shell-full of the juice of couch-grass together with garlic, and you will neither bruise nor tire however far you walk that day.

§ 57. If you wish to draw the drunkenness from a man, let him eat bruised Saffron in spring water.

§ 58. If you wish to be cheerful always, eat Saffron in food or drink, and you will never be sad; but beware of eating too much, lest you die of excessive joy.

12 PHYSICIANS OF MYDDVAI.

§ 59. If you wish not to be poisoned, drink a shellful of the juice of the herb called Christ's eyes; and it will not be easy to poison you. If you wish to be healthy always, drink a cup of the juice of mallows every day, and you will remain healthy always.

§ 60. If you wish to remain chaste every day, eat something of the herb called hyssop, and you will never be incited to the disturbance of lechery.

§ 61. Against prolapse of the womb (that is, its coming out), the chief remedy is to take wheat flour and bake it without eggs and with honey; and spread it on a hare's fur, and roast it under the embers, and drink night milk of a cow thereafter.

§ 62. If you wish that your teeth never ache at all, rub your gums within with your finger every day.

§ 63. Against a tumour, take a cockerel or a hen (according to the sex of the person, whether male or female) and place its rump, after plucking it, until the bird dies against it. And this will draw out the venom.

§ 64. Whoever wishes to remove warts, let the eyes of a day-old puppy, together with a dog's spine, be applied to them; and they will all fall off.

§ 65. Whoever wishes to destroy fleas, let wormwood be steeped in seawater for one hour; and then let it be dried in the sun. And when they are thoroughly dry, let them be scattered among the fleas; and they will be dead.

§ 66. To destroy flies, let pennywort be placed where they are accustomed to come, and those that come into contact with the herb will die.

§ 67. Against the bite of a snake, drink the juice of the light one here, and it will purge all the venom.

§ 68. Whoever loses their senses or their speech, let them drink the juice of primroses from within where the loss occurred; and they will truly be healed.

PHYSICIANS OF MYDDVAI. 13

§ 69. Whoever wishes to know what is in the womb of a pregnant woman, whether it be a boy or a girl, let him observe her as she sits and as she stands; and if her right foot moves first, it indicates a boy; if the left, a girl.

§ 70. If you wish to know the difference between a woman and a virgin who have not washed in water, give her some to drink; and if she is a woman she will immediately urinate; if a virgin, she will not do so any sooner than before.

§ 71. If you wish that the cockerel should not crow, anoint his comb with oil and he will be mute.

§ 72. For a film over the eye, let the juice of ivy be placed upon it; the film will break, and the eye will become clear.

§ 73. The little child that keeps crying; let his gums be rubbed with marrow until he becomes less fretful.

§ 74. If there be a cyst in a dangerous place on a person, and you wish to move it from its place; it is moved thus: take leaves of figwort and scatter them on the side toward which you wish it to move; and it will flee from the herbs placed on the other side.

§ 75. In the month of January do not let blood; drink three bowlfuls of wine on an empty stomach; seek medical herbs; make use of the flesh of wild goats and good herbs.

§ 76. In the month of February let blood from the thumb of the left hand; seek a regimen and medicines; and that will make the eyes good.

§ 77. In the month of March make use of ointment and the roots of herbs, and of liniment, frequently rather than letting blood. Do not take violent exercise, for cold will follow. Drink sweet wine on an empty stomach.

§ 78. In the month of April let blood; take light exercise; eat fresh meat; make use of warm drink; eat twice daily two mouthfuls of ox tongue; avoid the roots of herbs for they cause bloating; drink bitter infusion.

§ 79. In the month of May eat nothing of the head or feet of any animal; make use of warm drink; eat twice daily two mouthfuls

14 PHYSICIANS OF MYDDVAI.

on the tongue when you are fasting. Take a light, easy vomit; make use of cold whey. Drink the juice of fennel and wormwood.

§ 80. The month of June. Take a vial of cold water on your fast each day; drink neither ale nor mead; drink scalded milk. That is the regimen.

§ 81. The month of July, do not let blood; take a vomit, make use of the flowers of good herbs; guard carefully against lechery.

§ 82. The month of August. Make use of broth; and of herbs; drink neither ale nor mead; take white pepper in Crete [vinegar].

§ 83. The month of September, take three sips of milk first thing each day; all things that can be taken then may be taken, for the herbs and fruits will be ripe at that time; and bread in moderation.

§ 84. The month of October, make use of new wine. Eat the husks. Take a vomit. Eat fresh meat and good herbs.

§ 85. The month of November. Take no emetic; for at this time every person's blood will have congealed within them, which is dangerous. Then the head and the scurf will be troubled; and all the herbs.

§ 86. The month of December. Do not drink the broth, nor the red leaves of the broth; nor the footwashings, for these will diminish your blood.

§ 87. Whoever lets blood on the second day of the fifteenth of March, neither the ague nor consumption will come upon him in that year.

§ 88. Whoever lets blood on the third day of April, he will have no pain in his head nor fever in that year, unless he breaks his fast wrongly.

§ 89. And it is also good on the eleventh day of that month to let blood. And it is also good to let blood on the fourth or fifth day of the month of May.

§ 90. Whoever lets blood on the second day of

fifteen [from the fifteenth] of September, the fever or the cough or the consumption will not afflict him that year.

§ 91. The third Monday of January and the first Monday of February, and the second Monday of the month of October: whoever lets blood on those days risks dying from it. There are three days in the year; and on those days it is not proper to let blood from anyone, nor to take a medicinal drink. That is to say, the last day of April, the first Monday of August, and the last Monday of September.

§ 92. Whoever lets blood on those days will be dead by the fifteenth or the seventh day. And this is the reason. The veins will be full at those times; and if one takes a medicinal drink, it is dangerous. And if it is flesh-meat, he will be dead on the third day, or else he will be gravely ill for a fortnight, or else he will die on those aforesaid days by a sudden death.

§ 93. Good scholars have learned this and written it down; that is to say, that there are thirty-two dangerous nights in the year. And know, whoever is born on one of them, he will not live long. And whoever is betrothed on one of them will die without long delay, or else will live through pain and poverty. And whoever begins a business on one of them will not finish it well. Of those days in January there are seven: that is to say, the first and second, the fourth and fifth, the tenth and fifteenth, and the seventeenth.

In February there are three: the sixteenth, the seventeenth, and the eighteenth.

In March there are three: the fifteenth, the sixteenth, and the eighteenth.

In April there are two: the third, and the sixteenth.
