16 THE PHYSICIANS OF MYDDVAI.

In May there are four: the fifteenth, the sixteenth, the seventeenth, the twentieth, and the twenty-first.

In June there is one; and that is the second.

In the month of July there are two: the fifteenth and the seventeenth.

In August there are two: the eighteenth and the twentieth.

In the month of September there are two: the sixteenth and the eighteenth.

In the month of October there is one: the sixth.

In the month of December there are two: the fifteenth and the twentieth.

In the month of November there are three: the sixteenth, the seventeenth, and the eighteenth.

Whoever doubts these sayings, let him know that he is no wiser than the one who first learned them.

§ 94. For vomiting within the womb or hardening, boil flax through goat's milk and apply it frequently.

§ 95. To bring down swelling of the feet and legs: take the root of greater plantain with its bark and boil it through water; and when it has boiled, skim off the top, then take the middle portion and mix old lard with it; apply it on a cloth or rag to the feet or legs where the swelling is, and it will go away.

§ 96. For vomiting or pain in the throat: grind the root of celandine and the herb of lungwort and fennel and heads of garlic; and vinegar or wine and butter, and bind it around your neck; and this will reduce the pain and the vomiting.

§ 97. For bleeding of the nostrils, boil garlic in buttermilk; and drink it — it is proven.

§ 98. For a burn on any limb: take the root of white lily and wash it well, and boil it firmly through water; then crush

PHYSICIANS OF MYDDVAI. 17

very fine: and mix with oil; and a little egg white, and apply that on linen: and put it on the wound morning and night: and the more of that plaster there is, the better.

Another for a scald: scrape a clean spot, and scatter the ash upon it. and that will make it well. Another is to burn fern and mix that ash with white of egg: or else oil: and anoint with it; and that will make it well speedily and without scarring.

§ 99. A medicine against wildfire: for that is the bad flesh that does not appear until the end of three days: take good cheese and pound it firmly: and mix with honey until it is clear; and rub it in frequently: and apply upon it the leaves of broth-kale: and nothing will be seen of it by the end of the three days.

§ 100. For the bite of a mad dog; pound the elder and lard together: or pound onions with sour wine, or fennel seed and honey and apply it thereon.

§ 101. For pain of the breasts; pound the root of the greulys. and old lard. and apply it to them.

§ 102. The man who loses his senses. take the eye of the day. and the brooklime. and the sage (i. saies.) and beat them in wine; and give the patient fifteen doses to drink.

§ 103. If the belly is so hardened that one cannot go to stool; take flaxseed with water, and then boil it firmly in a cauldron. And then put it in a pan with much of fat. and cumin, and eat that as porridge.

§ 104. For palsy, take the brooklime and pound it. and strain the juice into a small vessel, and give the patient to drink at dawn on Christmas Day.

§ 105. For bleeding of both nostrils. take as much as you can pinch between three fingers of betony well ground in salt, and put it in the nostrils. and it will stop it speedily.

§ 106. If a man has suffered from a pain in his side: take in the morning, when the sun rises (while saying your prayers), the dew and smear him with a fresh cloth: and give the patient the amount of nine doses to drink.

§ 107. For coughing: grind bitter elder-berries and boil the juice in boiled milk, and strain it, and use it.

Another is: boil a potful of water until it reduces by half. Then mix rye flour with it, and put butter in it, and use it as a poultice.

§ 108. To kill parasites in the stomach or womb: take the juice of turnips and apply it; and they will come out. Another is: take a handful of peach bark from the ground dry, and drink it on an empty stomach with goat's milk, and they will all come out.

§ 109. To reduce hardness of the belly: put salt and silver; an equal quantity of each together; and place on the fire in a cauldron; and keep it on the fire until it becomes like wax in consistency. Make cakes of this, and place them against the man's back.

§ 110. For a snake bite: drink the juice of elecampane together with oil and salt. The juice of brooklime also, after being pressed and strained, counteracts poison.

Another is: take the brains of a red cockerel and put them in buttermilk, or fresh milk, or wine to drink: and put some of the breast meat warm against the bite, and that will draw out the poison, keeping the cockerel alive.

§ 111. For worms: take milk from a cow that has a bull-calf suckling; and barley flour and honey: and boil in a pan until it becomes pottage, and apply it warm against the abdomen.

Another is: make bread of barley and peeled hazelnuts, and eat it.

Another is: grind pure madder with brooklime, and drink the juice of it.

PHYSICIANS OF MYDDVAI. 19

§ 112. If a woman is unable to deliver her burden, let the leaves of the mugwort be rubbed against her thighs; and let them be removed speedily after she has delivered, lest they cause a flooding.

§ 113. For vomiting and pain in the knees: bruised madder, honey and salt, applied to it; and that will cure the swelling.

§ 114. For pain in the kidneys: pound the centaury in cold water and give it to the patient to drink.

§ 115. For excessive thirst: drink the centaury dissolved in warm water; this will break the thirst and purify the lungs.

§ 116. For a blister: take the ash of heather and the ash of bees or elder; and the ash of hart's horn and honey, and anoint it with that.

§ 117. For heartburn: take radish and boil it in goat's milk; drink it, and that will relieve it.

§ 118. For a burn from fire or water: place lily leaves inside boiling milk and lay it on the wound, until it is healed.

§ 119. For difficulty in urinating: take a hare's brain and rub it in fragrant wine, and drink it.

§ 120. For the bite of a serpent: put into the juice of fennel oil, or radish, or rue, or wormwood, and drink that, or eat it.

§ 121. For vomiting blood: boil woundwort in wine or milk and drink it; and that will stop it; or boil betony in goat's milk or wine, and that will stop it.

§ 122. For constipation: boil water with the roots of small woodland thistles and give that water to the patient to drink.

§ 123. Whoever is too fat, let him drink fennel, and that will reduce him.

§ 124. If one is angry, let him drink opium frequently, and that will calm the anger and produce joy.

§ 125. If a serpent has gone into a person's mouth, or if there are other living creatures inside him, let cattle dung be steeped in wine until thick, and drink that, and he will be freed of them.

§ 126. If worms are born within a person, or in the skin. Apply to him the roots of dragwort; and it will kill the worm immediately.

Another: spread the leaves of the pellitory on strong wine, and drink it for the throat.

§ 127. For eye-disease: drink a phial-full of the juice of the plantain, according to the prescription, and apply those herbs to the navel.

Another: spread the fumitory on wine, and drink it for the throat once. And they will all come out that same day.

§ 128. For a fever: drink the juice of rue and wine, and swallow three grains of coriander, and drink the opium through water (that is, through honey-water). And gather the plantain while saying the Lord's Prayer, and drink it then through wine and pepper. Take the juice of the comfrey after bruising it, and the juice of wormwood; mix them and apply with warm oil, and rub your body all over for three days on one side. And it will drive away the fever without fail.

§ 129. But if a man has a severe fever, cause him to go into a sweat, and protect him from the cold water on his arms; and take ivy of the earth and boil it firmly, and place it hot upon his head, and let blood from his arm; and he will be healed through the power of God.

§ 130. For vomiting and hiccups: apply a handful and a half of betony to warm water and drink it. To stop the vomiting: take the betony and boil it through mead. Pound it; and make from it four pellets; and give one each day for four days to drink during a fever.

§ 131. If a man takes poison, let him drink the juice of the pellitory and wine.

§ 132. To stop bleeding from the nostrils: take the tops of three nettles and bruise them together; and put that paste as far as you can into the nostrils. Another: take the fumitory, and pound it through sharp wine and put it in the nostrils, and it will stop the bleeding.

PHYSICIANS OF MYDDVAI. 21

§ 133. For vomiting: drink the juice of elder through warm wine and it will cure. Another remedy is to place the testicles inside a sharp vinegar.

§ 134. For pain from a swelling: take a cow's bladder, and breast milk and honey, and place it warm in your ears. That is a medicine that will not fail.

§ 135. These are the properties of the leek: It is good to drink the juice of the leek for vomiting blood. It is good for women who wish to have children to eat leeks frequently. It is good to take leek with wine against the bite of a snake, or another animal. It is good as a plaster of leeks and honey against a wound. For the aged and the young, the juice of leeks with breast milk is good. The juice of leeks with a goat's bladder and honey in three parts for pain: and that to be placed warm in the ears, or in the nostrils. It is good against pain of the head. The leek with wine is good against pain of the kidneys. The leek is good for joining a bone together, and for ripening tumours. If the leeks are placed with salt upon a wound, it will close it quickly. If the leeks are eaten raw, they will cause drunkenness. They bring the blood of people who have it in them. They will drive away the poison of the intestines. § 136. For those who cannot retain either food or drink, but only vomit: take milfoil and beat it in warm wine, and give the patient some to drink.

§ 137. Against poison, take two nuts and three of

dried figs, a handful of rue leaves, and twenty-five grains of salt, and give it to the patient on an empty stomach.

§ 138. These are the things that are good against bad flesh; namely white alum, ground to powder, and apply it to the sore.

For the same condition: take a toad that can do nothing but crawl; and steep a rod in its slime. Another is: take a horse's jaw with all the teeth in it; and heat a cupful of it and mix it with pepper and with lard; and anoint with that. And temper through a sieve, and apply the plaster daily until the end of a fortnight.

Another is: take honey and egg yolk and orpiment; and fine wheat flour, and mix together and apply to it, twice daily. It is proven.

§ 139. Mustard: it is good for expelling moisture that causes illness. It is good taken with vinegar for the bite of a snake or toad. It is good for toothache. It purifies the brain, suppresses women's flowers, and stimulates appetite, and strengthens the stomach. § 140. For through the properties of urine one may recognize the faults of a person, their dangers and their diseases, from far and near. First we will show what urine is.

There are four kinds of substance in urine. The first is the juice that flows from the food through the body. The second is the intestines performing their function. The third is to receive the various humors of choler and phlegm. The fourth part is the kidneys: by serving those humors which are sent to the bladder: and from thence all the signs of disease may be seen: and therefore from the cause of the humor of the urine and its color, the bad signs may be distinguished from the good.

§ 141. If the urine be turbid, or like red wine, or like black wine, or like green wine, or like oil, or like blood; or the urine be like that of animals, and if it is appropriate, examine those necessary causes carefully, and consider them separately; one will know which of those humors prevails, whether phlegm, or choler, or blood, or melancholy. And it is necessary to collect the urine in a glass vessel, and leave it to rest until the next air; and then by the ray of the sun examine it and judge it according to the signs mentioned above. If the urine is black, it is necessary to purify that person through the best purgative available; and make frequent use of ointments and oils. And again examine the urine: and if it is like saffron and does not clear: know then

24 PHYSICIANS OF MYDDVAI.

to have a fever active in the person, following a burning from heat and drought. If the person is seen to be growing thin, and the veins open and full or reddish: and the trunk is of uniform color and sinople: it is blood that is the matter. And if from jaundice¹ blood is on the arm beneath them, he will get relief without harm. If the trunk is thick and very red, without brightness in the rays of the sun, and resembling blood, it indicates weakness and wasting² of the body, showing that this comes from excessive fever. If the trunk is dispersing, fever will last a long time and is a sign. If the trunk is red, or resembling rust, and seen to move frequently, the fever is severe. If the trunk is pale and green (if this is at the beginning of the illness³) or within two⁴ days after the crisis has passed; and seen growing thicker and thicker, it is surely a sign of death. If the signs are more numerous without diminishing, it will be a long illness. If there is cloudiness on the surface of the trunk, it is a sign of fever from then on. If the trunk is disturbed during a hot fever, and darkening; pain in the head and shoulders, and weakening of hearing are indicated; and if relief does not come by the seventh day, he will die. If the trunk resembles oil in a hot fever, that indicates death or madness or dropsy. And if it moves quickly, it shows that a tumor on the brain is present. If there is a custom of it being fiery in color and pain when urinating, that indicates that food and drink do not agree with him, and for that reason the use of soft foods is necessary. If it is black or red, with sediment like red particles in the bottom, and the bladder failing, and pain in the kidneys, and pain in urinating, that person will be in danger. If urination is frequent and each time with a little pain, it is a sign of a stone. If the trunk⁵ is blue-white in a hot fever, or foamy, or red, and blood comes from both nostrils, that will be great danger. People who are weak in the chest, if their trunk is white, bloodletting is likely to help; and if it moves in the

§ 142. Blood ought to be let when the colour changes: for if it goes out dark, let it run until it becomes red. If it be thick, let it run until it is thin. If it be turbid, let it run until it is thick.

§ 143. To keep yourself always healthy, drink spoonfuls of the juice of mallow every day first thing.

§ 144. To calm wildness of birds or chicks, put a candle near where they are, and they will grow quiet.

§ 145. For a film over the eye, apply to it the juice of ground ivy.

§ 146. To ward off drunkenness, drink saffron in spring water.

§ 147. For the chest, apply to it the caul of a hen or a cock that has died.

§ 148. Against the falling sickness: kill a dog without the person's knowledge, put its bladder in his mouth; he will never have it again.

§ 149. To know whether a sick person will live: place a violet on his temples; if he sleeps he will live; if he does not sleep, he will die.

§ 150. If you wish that a woman shall not feel desire for you, eat rue in the morning.

§ 151. To break a bladder stone, take saxifrage, that is, tormaen, which grows in rocky places (for it is from that property that it got its name), and steep it in wine and pepper, and drink it warm; this will break the stone, and cause urination, and will cause women to menstruate; and it heals the kidneys and the bladder.

§ 152. These are the three vital thick organs: the liver, the kidneys, and the heart. And that is why they are so called. It is certain that where a disease strikes one of the three, it cannot be remedied without death speedily following.

§ 154. There are three long bones in the body: the kneecap, the ribs, and the lungs: for when the skin has been broken on one of these, it is certain that no physician knows when he will be able to restore him to health.

§ 155. For the riders' disease. Apply lime of peacock and the root of fern: and he will be well.

§ 156. For the bite of a mad dog; it is good to eat the root of agrimony.

§ 158. What is the greatest medicine: drawing a bone out safely from the brain.

§ 160. For the stitch: seek the spice-seller's remedy; that is the best against all pain.

§ 161. For a spot on the eye: take the white of an egg with the yolk removed, and spread it thickly on the eyelid; and take dust and an adder's slough and place it on the eyelid. This will heal it if done before sleep.

§ 171. Let everyone know that nothing can be obtained except through strength; there is no strength without health; there is no health without moderation in one's nature: there will be no moderation in one's nature unless the heat in the members is kept in balance: God ordained the proper rule by which a man should keep his health, and showed it to the philosophers, his servants, and to the prophets, his chosen ones, who are filled with the Holy Spirit; and God endowed them with that art.

§ 172. The Latins, and the men of Persia, and the Greeks — from these we chose and loved: from these we sought and pondered upon. And therefore let everyone know that God gave the supreme knowledge to the men of Greece to understand every art, and the nature of every thing above all other nations; and the means of preserving a man's health.

§ 173. The philosophers and the wise men foresaw that man was made of four elements, and each one of them has its contrary, for which food and drink are needed at all times; and if he does not get them he will fail: if a man takes too much or too little food or drink, the body will weaken and fall into disease; and also in many contrary respects. But if he takes food and drink in due measure, the body will strengthen, and health will be preserved likewise.

§ 174. The philosophers say that whoever eats

or who sleeps more or less than is proper, or who labours more or less than is proper, or who rests more or less than is proper. Those who give themselves up to ease or to hardship to excess, or those who make use of bleeding beyond what is proper, without due consideration, transgress against temperance. These are the things we treat of briefly, and concerning what is best for these purposes.

§ 175. Wise men have said: whosoever abstains from excess in eating and drinking, and adopts moderation in food and drink, as nature directs, shall have health and long days; for that is a long life. Philosophers have never said otherwise. Joy and love, and the receiving of worldly honour — these strengthen and support life, if they arise from moderation. And therefore, whoever desires to live and to continue, let him seek that which is lasting, and that which preserves life.

§ 176. Whoever desires life, it is necessary for him to restrain his appetite, and not to eat excess upon excess. I heard Hippocrates, in preserving his life, through that means overcome much weakness and old age; and then his disciples said to him: You are the greatest teacher in wisdom; had you eaten or drunk more, the weakness which is upon you would not be there? Then Hippocrates answered: My sons, said he, I eat just enough for my life to continue; we should not live to eat more frequently than is needed to maintain a man's life. It is not for food's sake that one should seek to continue; for I have seen many die from eating too frequently.

§ 177. Restrain the appetite for gluttony, and eat slowly; those who do so will be long-lived; and in this way one may

proved. The men of Arabia are known among those whose nature is lean and spare, and of barren land; those people will be long-lived; and this comes from the moderate use of foods and drink. The lean body has two means of health: First, that the use of foods be moderate to the age and nature — namely, to accustom oneself to foods and drink of a similar kind, and to be nourished upon them. The second is that the contents of the stomach pass out by the highest passage available to it.

§ 178. Moreover, let everyone know that the bodies of people are contrary to foods taken by the lake: and that each one of them tends toward sickness. Also corrupt are the bodies through great heat of the sun, that which dries the organs: and especially the bodies of animals upon which those people are fed. When the body is hot, strong foods are proper to it, for they are easy to digest.

§ 179. When the body is strong, and dry, gentle foods are proper to it; and moist foods; for those the body digests easily. In this way a person best learns to maintain his health, using foods and drink that are suited to his nature. Let this be proved.

§ 180. If a man has a hot-natured body, hot foods are proper to him.

§ 181. If the body be of a cold nature, cold foods are proper to it.

§ 182. Moreover, for a moist body, or a dry body of such nature, cold foods are forbidden.

§ 183. A hot stomach finds strong foods best for it, for such a stomach is likened to a fire that would burn

of the ribs. A stomach that is cold by nature will find warm foods most beneficial; for such foods are likened to fire burning grass.

§ 184. The signs of a healthy stomach are these: that the body is nimble, that the understanding is clear, and that food is frequently desired.

§ 185. The signs of an unhealthy stomach are these: heaviness of body, loss of feeling in it, laziness in action; paleness of face, a weak and languid look, and irritability of temper; and when these things are heard of as complaints; for they breed foul humors in the stomach; which spread through the body to all its members, and cause loathing of food.

§ 186. When you rise from your bed, stretch yourself, then extend your limbs, moving your head and your neck. This strengthens the body, and the movement of the head causes the natural moisture to run from the stomach to the brain; and if the brain falls asleep again the body sinks back. In summer, bathe the face in cold water: this preserves the heat in the head, and from that the appetite is nourished. After that, put fair clothing on yourself: for a man's mind is gladdened by fair things, and the heart is lifted. After that, dry your teeth and beware of losing them to decay, for they will be the cleaner for it; and your speech will be clearer, and your breath purer. Also, stand still at times; for that does great good, and opens the creature, and the neck is strengthened. The complexion of the face is improved and the arms are strengthened, and the sight is brightened, and it makes you more active, and strengthens the memory. Conversation and walking together after you have eaten and drunk in moderation; and labor sufficiently by walking or riding; for this strengthens the body — and destroys the foul humors in the stomach; and a man will be more vigorous and stronger, and his stomach will be more digestive, and his sinews more supple.

§ 187. When you take food, eat as much of the best as you can get; and especially sour bread; for the foods of a weak and watery quality are slow to digest in the stomach. Other than two kinds of food; weak food and strong food; eat the strong food first; for the heat of the stomach is thereby increased. And that is not surprising: for the liver, which is nearest to it, receives its warmth from it.

§ 188. When you eat, do not eat your fill entirely; leave some appetite remaining in you. Do not drink water along with your food; for it chills the stomach, and hinders the digestion of the food, and extinguishes the heat. And if you must drink water, drink a little, and only the cold water you can get. When you have finished eating, walk a short distance. When you wish to sleep, do not sleep too much; rest an hour on the right side, and then turn to the left side and complete your sleep. If you feel pain in your stomach and heaviness, place many clothes beneath you to draw the heat to the stomach; and drink warm water, which causes the impurity that is in your stomach to be vomited up. Exercise much before eating warms the stomach. Exercise after eating harms the stomach; for without the labour of digestion the heat of the stomach fails, and from that many diseases arise. Sleeping before eating makes a person lean; sleeping after eating makes one strong. The night is colder than the day. And for that reason the stomach digests sooner by night than by day; for when the weather is cold, the heat gathers from the limbs around the stomach. If a person has been accustomed to eating twice a day, and then eats only once, that harms the stomach. If one has been accustomed to eating once a day, and then eats twice, that likewise harms the stomach. If one eats at a set time each day, and changes that to another time, that is harmful to the stomach. Except from necessity; if it is needful to change, do so gradually. Also, do not eat until

...that the stomach may become empty, and this you may know by your desire for food, and the thinness of your complexion. If you eat without having an appetite for food, the cold will extinguish your natural heat. But if you eat when you do have an appetite for food, your nature will be as warm as fire. And whoever does not take food there, his stomach will fill with the sickness that causes the blood to go to the head.

INTRODUCTION.

§ 1. Here, by the help of God, the supreme chief Sovereign, are shown the most notable and principal methods of healing the human body. The persons who caused these to be written in this manner were Rhiwallon the Physician and his sons, Kadwgan, Griffith, and Einion. For they were the most able and eminent physicians of their time, and of the time of Rhys Gryg, their lord and the lord of Dinevor — the nobleman who upheld their rights and privileges with complete integrity and honour, as was fitting. The reason they caused a record of their skill to be committed to writing was so that no one who came after them should be found lacking the necessary knowledge that they possessed.

THE HEAD.

§ 2. The head is the first and most important part of the human body, which God formed, for within it reside the five bodily senses.

ORIGIN OF DISEASES IN THE HEAD.

Section 3. Diseases originate in three places in the head: one is the pericranium, the second is the cranium, and the third is the dura mater.

PRESERVATION OF THE CRANIUM AND SCALP.

Section 4. The cranium is preserved by making an incision in the scalp down to the cranium, allowing the venom to escape. The scalp is preserved by bloodletting and cauterization.

DURA MATER — TREATMENT.

Section 5. To treat the dura mater, expose it, then take two parts of wood betony and three parts of violet, pound them together with salted butter, and apply the mixture to the area. This will draw out the venom from the dura mater and will reduce any inflammation and pain present there.

DURATION OF TREATMENT.

Section 6. From the time the scalp is laid open until nine days have passed, this opening should remain on the bone. That is to say, this approach should be followed in a longstanding complaint of the head.

WOUND ON THE HEAD — TREATMENT. PHYSICIAN'S FEE.

Section 7. In the case of a recent blow or fresh wound to the head, it should be treated as soon as possible, to prevent blood from pooling on the dura mater and becoming infected there. When the bone and the dura mater are exposed, take violet and fresh butter and pound them together. If violet cannot be obtained, take egg whites and linseed, pound them together; or use fresh butter and linseed, and apply until the pain subsides. Then an ointment should be prepared from herbs, butter, and tallow,

and applied thereto until it is cured. A pound is the physician's fee for this treatment as a deed of mercy alone, without food included: or nine score pence (180 pence) with food.¹

PAIN IN THE EYE. CAUTERY.

§ 8. For pain in the eye. Applying a hot cautery to the hollow of the eyebrow, and another to the nape of the neck, is beneficial for discharge from the head.

WATERY EYE — TREATMENT.

§ 9. For a red, watery eye (inflammation of the eyelid margins with overflow of tears), insert a seton beneath the jaw, and apply a hot cautery to the nape of the neck; this is beneficial for discharge from the head.

DISEASED EYELIDS — REMEDY.

§ 10. For a dry, scaly condition of the eyelids: Take the juice of the strawberry, hen's fat, and May butter. Pound them well together and keep the mixture in a horn or box. At bedtime, anoint your eye and eyelids thoroughly with it, and they will be cured.

PNEUMONIA — TREATMENT.

FEVERS

Section 12. There are four kinds of fevers that originate in summer: latent fever, intermittent fever, ephemeral fever, and inflammatory fever. The fifth fever is typhus, and this type originates in the brain. A latent fever is relieved by an emetic, a cordial, and cauteries. It arises from the excessive production of thick humor in the stomach, which results in loss of appetite and fatigue during summer. Mugwort, madder, meadow sweet, milfoil, hemp, red cabbage, and tutsan — all seven of these herbs enter into the composition of the medicine pre-

required. Whoever obtains all of them will not suffer long from a wounded lung, nor need fear for his life. Any of the following herbs may also be added: butcher's broom, agrimony, tutsan, dwarf elder, amphibious persicaria, centaury, birthwort, field scabious, peppermint, daisy, knapweed, roots of the red nettle, crakeberry, St. John's wort, privet, wood betony, roots of the yellow goat's beard, heather, water avens, woodruff, leaves of the earthnut, agrimony, wormwood, bastard balm, small burdock, and orpine.

INTERMITTENT FEVERS. TREATMENT.

Section 13. For intermittent fevers: Take dandelion and fumitory, steeped in water, first thing in the morning. Then around noon take wormwood steeped in water in the same way, drinking it up to ten times, the dose being served warm. Also take bread made from pounded wheat, or oatcakes, goat's whey, the flesh of a young bird, and thick porridge in water, avoiding milk and all dairy foods. If the fever does not then stop, the patient must be placed in a bath when the attack comes on, and given an emetic while in the bath, as it will then work more powerfully.

COOLING DRINKS.

Section 14. The three best cooling drinks are apple water, goat's whey, and spring water.

INTERMITTENT FEVERS.

§ 16. There are two kinds of hemorrhoids: humoral hemorrhoids and inflamed hemorrhoids. The latter are caused by summer heat, the former by summer moisture, when either condition predominates. This is how the condition arises. Four veins run from the liver to the anus, and so the condition may be treated as follows: secure three of these veins with a ligature and leave the fourth free. The cautery should also be applied to the ankles, and around the knees and the backs of the thighs. In this way the blood will be consistently redirected to the lower limbs, once the cauteries have drawn all the excess fluid from the vein.

ABDOMINAL COMPLAINTS — ASCITES, PERITONITIS, ABDOMINAL TUMOR, TYMPANITIS. TREATMENT OF PERITONITIS. EMETIC. EXTRACT OF STINKING HELLEBORE. INTERNAL ABDOMINAL TUMOR — TREATMENT.

§ 17. There are four kinds of abdominal complaints: ascites, peritonitis, abdominal tumor, and tympanitis. Ascites cannot be cured. Tympanitis is likewise a condition from which there is no escape, though it is not quickly fatal. Peritonitis is treated with an emetic, the blue confection, and a medicine. The herbs required for the medicine are: sweet gale, bay leaves, pimpernel, male speedwell, river startip, borage, moss, liverwort, the young leaves of the earth nut, and mallow. The emetic mentioned above should be prepared as follows. Take stinking hellebore freshly dug from the ground by the root, wash it well, slice it thin, then bruise it as thoroughly as possible in a mortar, discarding the spent pulp after the juice has been pressed out. The juice should then be placed in a pan over the fire and boiled until ebullition ceases and it is nearly solid. Keep it as long as you wish, and form it into small pills when you are ready to give it to the patient. Abdominal tumor is cured by means of cauteries, issues, a cordial, and an emetic.

Section 18. Warts will often form around the anus. The best way to remove them is to cut them out with cold iron, then cauterize the site and anoint it with honey.

THREE KINDS OF URINARY DISORDERS. STRANGURY. HOT AIR BATH. BLADDER STONE — OPERATION. SUBSEQUENT TREATMENT. PREPARATORY TREATMENT. GRAVEL — TREATMENT.

Section 19. There are three kinds of painful urinary disorders. Strangury is cured by means of an emetic, a cordial, cauterization, and a dry hot-air bath. A hard bladder stone is removed by the following operation. Take a staff and place it in the bend of the knee, then secure both arms inside the knees, folding them over the staff, and tie both wrists together with a band behind the neck. The patient is placed on his back, stomach facing up, with some support under both thighs, and the stone is cut out on the left side of the urethra. Afterward, the patient should be placed in a water bath on the same day and again early the following day, after which he should be placed in the kyffeith. He should then be moved to his bed and laid on his back, his wound cleaned and dressed with flax and salted butter. He should be kept at a constant temperature until it is known whether he will recover from the effects of the operation. He should be kept without food or drink for a day and a night before the operation, and should have a bath beforehand. If the condition is gravel, prepare a medicine from the following herbs macerated in strong clear wheat ale: water pimpernel, tutsan, meadowsweet, St. John's wort, ground ivy, agrimony, milfoil, birch, common burnet, columbine, motherwort, laurel, gromwell, betony, borage, dandelion, little field madder, amphibious persicaria, and liverwort.

Section 98. For burns occurring anywhere on the body: Take the root of the white lily, wash it clean, and boil it briskly in water. Then reduce it to a pulp, mix with oil and a little egg white, and spread it on lint. Apply this night and morning. The more of this plaster you apply, the better.

Another method: Burn ivy in a clean place, and cover the burn with its ashes; it will heal the burn quickly.

Another way is to burn fern and mix the ashes with egg white, or alternatively with oil, then anoint the burn with it. It will heal quickly and remarkably well.

NETTLE RASH, OR ERYSEPELATOUS ERETHEMA. TREATMENT.

Section 99. A remedy for nettle rash (when it indicates a poor constitution), so that it may clear up within three days: Take good cheese and pound it briskly in a mortar. Mix honey with it until it becomes transparent. Anoint the affected area with this frequently, placing a cabbage leaf over it, and it will have disappeared within three days.

BITE OF A MAD DOG. TREATMENT.

Section 100. For the bite of a mad dog: Pound ground ivy well in a mortar with lard, or pound leeks with vinegar, or fennel seed and honey together, and apply to the wound.

INFLAMMATION OF THE BREASTS.

Section 101. For inflammation of the breasts: Pound the roots of tutsan with rancid lard and apply to the affected area.

INSANITY — TO CURE.

Section 102. When a man becomes insane, take daisy, field southernwood, and sage, steep them in wine, and let the patient drink it for fifteen days.

OBSTINATE CONSTIPATION — HOW TO OVERCOME IT.

Section 103. If the bowels become so constipated that they cannot be moved, take duckweed, boil it briskly in a pot, then transfer it to a pan and fry it with a quantity of blood and butter, and eat it hot.

PALSY — HOW TO CURE IT.

Section 104. For palsy: take field southernwood, pound it in a mortar, and strain out the juice to about a small cupful. Give it to the patient to drink at the dawn of Christmas Day.

NOSEBLEED — REMEDY.

Section 105. For a nosebleed: take as much betony as you can hold between three fingers, grind it thoroughly with salt, and place it in your nostrils. This will stop the bleeding quickly.

Section 106. If a man's liver adheres to his ribs, go out at sunrise, reciting the Lord's Prayer, and gather river star tip. Steep it in fresh ale and give it to the patient to drink while he is in a bath, continuing for nine days.

COUGH — REMEDY AND ALTERNATIVE METHOD.

Section 107. For a cough: bruise hemp agrimony in a mortar, mix the juice with boiling milk, strain it, and use it.
Alternative method: Boil a pot of water until it is reduced by half. Mix rye meal into it, add butter, and eat it hot.

WORMS — HOW TO DESTROY THEM. ALTERNATIVE METHOD.

Section 108. To destroy worms in the stomach or bowels: take the juice of turnips, apply it as a fomentation, and the worms will come out.

Another method is to take a handful of bark from a peach tree growing in dry ground, and drink it while fasting with goat's milk, and the worms will all come out.

CONSTIPATION — HOW TO OVERCOME IT — SUPPOSITORY.

§ 109. To overcome constipation: Take salt and second milk in equal parts, place them on the fire in an evaporating dish, and leave until the mixture is reduced to a soft, wax-like mass. Then form this into cakes (suppositories) and insert them into the patient's rectum.

SNAKEBITE — ANTIDOTES. ANOTHER METHOD.

§ 110. For the bite of a snake: Drink the juice of greater plantain with oil and salt. The juice of mugwort, when bruised and strained, will also neutralize the poison.

Another method is to take the brains of a red cockerel and rue, mix with sweet milk, curdled milk, or wine, and drink. Also take flesh from the breast of the cockerel while it is still warm (and still alive) and apply it to the wound. This will draw out the venom.

WORMS — A POULTICE — A REMEDY. ANOTHER METHOD.

§ 111. For worms: Take milk from a cow that has a bull calf nursing from her, add barley meal and honey, and boil it in a pan like porridge. Apply this hot to the stomach.

Another method is to make bread from barley and shelled nut kernels, and eat it.

Another approach is to bruise fresh rue and mugwort in a mortar and drink the juice.

DIFFICULT LABOR — HOW TO ASSIST.

§ 112. If a woman is unable to give birth to her child, bind mugwort to her left thigh. Remove it immediately once she has delivered, to prevent hemorrhage.

PAIN IN THE KIDNEYS — A REMEDY.

EXTREME THIRST — HOW TO HELP.

SMALLPOX — A TREATMENT.

A SURFEIT — HOW TO RELIEVE IT.

A BURN OR SCALD — A REMEDY FOR.

RETENTION OF URINE — A REMARKABLE REMEDY.

Section 119. For retention of urine: Take the brains of a hare and mix them with wine. Let the patient smell it for an hour and then drink it.

POISON — ANTIDOTE.

URINAL PATHOLOGY.—FOUR URINARY ELEMENTS.

§ 140. From the condition of a man's urine, one may distinguish his defects, dangers, fevers (plagues,) and diseases, whether he be present or absent. However, we should first show what the composition of urine is. It contains four fundamental elements.

FIRST. The humor of the blood which circulates in the reproductive organs.

* The following is the translation of an extract on the same subject, purporting to have been made from the Book of "Hywel ddu Feddyg," a descendant of Einion ab Rhiwallon, by "Ieinō ap Wm. ap ff," A.D. A thousand, [date notation in abbreviated form].

"The following are the basic rules of urine examination. If the urine shows a yellow color of a faint golden hue, or if it has the color of refined gold, it indicates that food and drink are perfectly digested in the stomach.
If it is a fiery red, like the sunset in the west—if red like oriental saffron—if a fiery red like a vanishing flame—if red like a piece of consuming fire; these four colors indicate that the food and drink have left the stomach so that their digestion may be completed.
If urine is deep colored like human liver, or the color of blushing cheeks, like strained red wine, or greenish like the mane of oxen; these three colors together indicate that food and drink are properly digested in the stomach.
If water has a leaden hue, or an intensely black color like black ink, or a dead black like black horn; these three colors indicate the death of the man.
If it has the color of clear spring water, or an opaline color like transparent horn, or the color of plain milk, or the hue of camel hair; these four colors indicate that the food in the stomach has not been digested.
If it has a greenish blue color, this indicates that the patient should be allowed less food and drink.
If it is the color of poorly bled meat, it indicates that digestion of food has begun in the stomach.
If it has a greenish hue like an unripe apple, or the hue of a ripe apple; these two colors indicate that the food and drink are half digested in the stomach. And thus it ends."
These extracts, as well as the teaching of our "Meddygon" on the same subject, are of very little value, except insofar as they show how crude and empirical the urinary diagnosis and pathology of our ancestors was. The first writer on urine examination was Theophilus, called Philaretus, a monk who was Physician to Heraclius, who reigned in the first half of the 7th century. His treatise on urine has little originality, other than being the first of a class of writings distinguished above all others for deception and nonsense. After him we find a succession of authors (particularly the urine specialists of the middle ages) pursuing fanciful speculations to a greater pitch of absurdity than can be readily imagined by those whose curiosity has not led them to explore the byways of medicine. In no area has modern medical research made greater advances than urinary diagnosis and pathology, thanks to the microscopist and the chemist. See "Lilium medicinæ" of Bernard Gordon— Watson (of New York) on ancient medicine.

URINAL DIAGNOSIS

§ 141. Should the urine be abundant in water, or resemble red, black, or green wine, or oil, or blood, or the urine of animals, a skilled person who carefully studies the essential causes will understand which of the humors chiefly predominates — whether phlegm, bile, blood, or black bile. It is necessary that the urine be collected in a glass vessel and left to settle until the second hour, when, by the light of the sun, the physician should judge what it indicates.

SIGNS IN ORDER — BLACK URINE

i. If the urine is black, it will be necessary to restore that patient's constitution by the most skillful means possible, frequently using baths and oil. The urine should then be examined again, and if it appears saffron-colored and turbid, know that the person has a painful disease produced by heat and dryness.

SINOPLE

ii. If the patient is wasting away and clearly declining in strength, with prominent veins or a red (transparent) complexion, and the urine is a color similar to sinople (red-green), it arises from the blood. By bleeding the patient in the left arm, he will be restored with little difficulty.

THICK, OILY, OPAQUE AND BLOOD-TINGED.
iii. If the urine is thick, oily, deep red, not transparent when held up to sunlight, and blood-tinged, it indicates physical weakness and exhaustion caused by excessive fever.

CURDLED.
iv. If the urine appears curdled, it indicates a prolonged fever.

RED AND CHANGEABLE.
v. If the urine is red or sulfur-yellow, and seems to change its appearance frequently, it indicates a dangerous fever.

CLOUDY AND GREENISH — A CLOUD ON THE SURFACE.
vi. If the urine is cloudy and greenish at the onset of a fever, or within two days after, and when passed it grows progressively thicker, the patient will certainly die. If these symptoms multiply but the urine does not thicken, it indicates a drawn-out fever.
If there is a hazy, sky-like appearance on the surface of the urine, it indicates that a fever is coming.

FOUL URINE.
vii. If the urine appears foul during a fever, it indicates fever with inflammation, headache, pain in the shoulders, and deafness. If the patient is not relieved within seven days, he will die.

OILY.
viii. If the urine looks like oil during the height of a fever, it indicates death, delirium, or erysipelas. If the condition is not quickly resolved, it points to a softening of the brain.

FIERY, AND PASSED WITH PAIN.
ix. If the urine takes on a fiery color and is passed with pain, this indicates that the patient's food and drink are not being properly

digested. It is accordingly expedient in such a case for the patient to restrict himself to liquid food.

BLACK OR RED, WITH SEDIMENT.

x. If the urine is black or red, and there is sediment at the bottom, along with difficulty urinating, pain in the kidneys, and pain when passing urine, the patient is in danger. If the urine is passed frequently and in small amounts, this indicates a stone in the bladder.

xi. If the urine is bluish white during a fever, or reddish brown or red, accompanied by nosebleeds, it is a sign of great danger.

WHITE.

xii. In persons with a diseased liver, when thin urine turns white, it indicates future suffering; but if it clears up suddenly, it indicates a boil.

xiii. If during a fever the urine takes on the color of bile, being thick with a whitish cloud and whitish granules floating in it, this indicates a prolonged and lingering illness.
xiv. If more urine is passed than is normal during a fever, and the color is poor, though it flows freely, this indicates imminent danger. If the urine is abnormal when passed but later takes on a healthy color, it indicates that the patient will waste away from future suffering.
xv. If a man in the grip of a fever passes urine that appears fairly normal but contains white gravel, and the fever does not decrease, this indicates danger.

CHASTITY.

§ 172. The Latins, the men of Persia and the Greeks say: what we choose we love, what we seek we think of. § 173. The philosophers and wise men foreknew that man was formed of four elements, each being antagonistic to the others, and each consequently requiring continual nourishment; which, if it does not obtain, it will succumb. If a man takes too much or too little food or drink, the body will become weak, fall into disease, and be open to injurious consequences. If he partakes temperately of food and drink, the body will gain strength, and health will also be preserved.

MODERATION.

§ 174. The philosophers have said that whoever eats or drinks more or less than he should, or sleeps more or less, or labours more or less — whether from idleness or from hardship (being obliged to over-exert himself) — or who, being accustomed to being bled, refrains from doing so, will without doubt not escape sickness. Of these things we shall treat presently, and of what is most suitable for our use.

SAYINGS OF THE WISE AS TO FOOD.

§ 175. Wise men have declared that whoever refrains from eating or drinking immoderately, and will only partake tem-

moderately of food and drink, as his constitution requires, shall enjoy health and long days, that is, a long life. Philosophers never said anything to the contrary. Desire, love, and the reception of worldly honour — these things fortify and assist life, so long as they are satisfied in moderation. For this reason, whoever desires life and its continuation should seek that which is lasting and tends to prolong life.

MODERATION AS A MEANS TO PROLONG LIFE — HIPPOCRATES AND HIS DISCIPLES.

Section 176. Whoever would prolong life should restrain his appetite and not eat excessively. I have heard that Hippocrates, having reached old age, during which he suffered greatly from infirmity and the burden of years, was addressed by his disciples as follows: "Thou great teacher of wisdom, if you had eaten and drunk abundantly, would you have had to endure all the weakness you now suffer?" Then Hippocrates replied: "My sons, I eat a proper portion given that I am alive. I would not be alive if, with the aim of merely prolonging human life, I had eaten too frequently. Eating is not the one thing needful when prolonging life is the goal, for I have seen many die from eating too much."

§ 179. When a man's body is fat and dry, rich and juicy food is appropriate for him, as it will be easily absorbed. In this way a man may maintain his health. He should restrict himself to food that suits his constitution. This has been proven.

A COLD HABIT.

§ 181. If a man's body is constitutionally cold, cold foods are appropriate for him.

A HUMID OR DRY HABIT.

§ 183. Strong food is most suitable for a hot stomach, since such a stomach can be compared to fire consuming loose flax. Weak food is most appropriate for a cold stomach, since such a stomach can be compared to fire consuming straw.

§ 184. The signs of healthy digestion are that the body is active, the mind is clear, and the appetite is frequent.

HOW TO BEHAVE UPON GETTING OUT OF BED, AND THROUGHOUT THE DAY, WITH OTHER MATTERS OF HYGIENE.

§ 186. When rising from bed, walk around for a while, stretch your limbs, and draw in your head and neck. This will strengthen your limbs, and the drawing in of the head will cause the vital spirits to rush from the stomach to the head; and from the head, when you sleep, they will descend to the stomach again. In summer, bathe in cold water, as this will maintain warmth in the head and stimulate an appetite for food. Then dress yourself in fine clothing, for a person's mind takes pleasure in fine things and the heart is thereby made lighter. Then clean your teeth with the dry bark of the hazel, as they will become all the fairer for it. Your speech will also be clearer and your breath sweeter. Good upright posture should be practiced regularly, as it will benefit you greatly — relieving pressure on the dura mater (the membrane of the brain), strengthening the neck, enhancing the appearance of the face, giving strength to the arms, improving your sight, protecting you from pallor, and sharpening your memory. Conversation, walking with others, and eating and drinking according to your usual habits should all be done in moderation. Take moderate exercise in walking or riding, as this will invigorate the body and relieve heartburn, so that a person will be more robust and strong, the stomach warmer, and the nerves more resilient.

WHAT TO EAT.

Section 187. When you eat, choose what you most enjoy if you can, particularly leavened bread. If you eat simple food it will be easier for the stomach to digest. If, though unaccustomed to it, you must eat two kinds of food — plain and rich — eat the rich first, for the lower part of the stomach is hotter than the upper, being nearer to the source of heat, and so more heat will be available there.

RULES FOR EATING AND DRINKING.

Section 188. When you eat, do not satisfy your appetite completely, but leave some desire for food remaining. Do not drink water with your food, as it will cool your stomach, hinder digestion, and extinguish its warmth. However, when you do drink water, drink it sparingly, choosing the coldest water available. When you have finished eating, take a walk on a level, well-sheltered piece of ground. When you feel like sleeping, do not sleep too much. Rest on your right side, then turn to the left and curl yourself up. If you feel pain in your stomach (heartburn) and heaviness, put on extra clothing in order to draw heat toward the stomach, and drink warm water, as this will induce vomiting and remove unhealthy matter from your stomach. Walking a great deal before eating will warm the stomach. Walking a great deal after eating will harm the stomach, because the food, being undigested due to the exertion, will fall to the lower part of the stomach and there give rise to many diseases. Sleeping before eating will make a person thin, but sleeping after eating will make a person fat. The night is colder than the day, and consequently the stomach will digest food more quickly by night than by day, because the colder the

In cold weather, the stomach digests better, as heat withdraws from the extremities and concentrates around the stomach. If a man who habitually eats twice a day eats only once, it will harm his stomach. Likewise, if a man who habitually eats only once a day eats twice, it will also be harmful. Changing the time at which one normally eats will also do harm to the stomach. If necessity ever requires a change in one's habits, let it be made gradually. Also, do not eat until the stomach is fully empty, which you can tell by the feeling of hunger and by your saliva becoming thin. If you eat without hunger, your body's warmth will diminish. If you eat when truly hungry, your vitality will burn like fire; and whoever fails to eat when genuinely hungry will find their stomach filling with harmful matter, which will cause headache.

TO MAKE HOLY WATER TO BRIGHTEN THE EYES AND TO CLEANSE THEM.

§ 65. Take roses, samphire, rue, the blessed oak, red fennel, maiden-hair, the deaf nettle, and celandine, and wild thyme, wash them clean and let them stand a day and a night in white wine, and after that distil over the surface of a brass pot, and the first water you get will be like silver, and that will be good against every kind of ailment of the eye, and against a film on the eye.

AGAINST WATERING OF THE EYES.

§ 66. Take the flowers of eyebright, and eat them, and this will brighten the eyes, and dry them so that they are clear.

ANOTHER.

§ 67. Anoint your eyes with the juice of celandine and fresh honey mixed together, and you will gain great benefit.

ANOTHER.

§ 68. Get white wine and the juice of celandine, and the juice of red fennel, and boil in the white wine until a third is reduced, and with that anoint your eyes, and this will keep them bright and healthy.

102 PHYSICIANS OF MYDDVAI.

AGAINST A THORN OR PAIN IN THE EYE.

§ 69. Take the yolk of an egg and wheat flour, with a little blue vitriol, and mix them together, spread on a linen cloth, and place against your eyes when going to sleep, and it will heal by the next day; let this be done until three days are past.

AGAINST PAIN IN A PERSON'S EYE.

§ 70. Take the gall of a hare, the gall of a crane, the gall of an eel, the gall of a stag, water of guyra, and vine leaves, and strike a blow upon ivy wood, and take the juice that comes out of the wood, mix it with the above things and boil a little, then strain through a fine linen cloth, and when it has cooled, put a little of it in the corners of your eyes, and it is a wonder if he who uses it cannot see the stars at midday, such is the virtue of this medicine.

TO STRENGTHEN THE EYE.

§ 71. Take eyebright, red rose leaves, and yellow-wort, pound them together and boil them in white wine, or old clear strong ale, boil them a good while, and strain cleanly through a fine cloth, and wash the eyes night and morning, and you will be healed.

TO KNOW OF A MAID WHETHER SHE HAS KEPT HER MAIDENHOOD OR NOT.

§ 72. Take the powder of the woodlouse and put it in her drink, and if she is not a maid, she will rise to make water; if she is a maid, she will not stir.

TO KNOW WHETHER THE CHILD IN A WOMAN'S WOMB IS A BOY OR A GIRL.

§ 73. Take the breast milk of the woman and put it upon her own urine; if the milk floats on top, it is a boy; if it sinks to the bottom, it is a girl.

PHYSICIANS OF MYDDVAI. 103

AGAINST THE PAIN OF A COLD, THAT IS RHEUMATISM, AND ALL
MANNER OF PAINFUL AILMENTS, AND WEAKNESS IN THE SHOULDERS,
ARMS, AND LEGS.

§ 74. Take wild thyme, and bruise it small, and boil it in the dregs of strong ale until it is thick, and apply it as hot as the patient can bear, and use this remedy for five days, and he will truly be well.

AGAINST A THORN.

§ 75. If a thorn enters a man's flesh, whether in his feet, or in his hand, and it cannot be gotten out, take the root of the black thistle, or its leaves, and the white of eggs, and fine flour of rye, or barley where there is no rye, and apply it as a plaster, and it will draw it out.

AGAINST THE SOFT AGUE OF THE SECOND DAY.

§ 76. Take a large handful of feverfew combs, a handful of the tips of year-old broom, and a handful of the watercress, and wash them clean, and bruise them in a mortar, and mix them with strong ale, and strain it, and drink it nine times fasting, and it will break the fever.

AGAINST INABILITY TO MAKE WATER.

§ 77. Seek the seed of broom and grind it fine like flour, and put it in drink and drink it, do this until you are well.

ANOTHER.

§ 78. Take the seed of broom, and count nine, casting the tenth to God, and grind the seed into fine pollen, and take it in drink, or else in boiled honey, and if a woman or maiden does this, no pain or abscess will ever come in her breast.

AGAINST A BRUISE.

§ 79. Take the dregs of old strong ale, and the tallow of a black wether, or goat's tallow, and wheat bran, and boil well, and apply to

104 PHYSICIANS OF MYDDVAI.

a cloth of wool as hot as can be endured applied to the wound three times, and it will be healed.

A DRINK AGAINST THE GREAT GOUT.

§ 80. Get hazel buds, sickle-wort, holy thistle, and the blessed oak, a measure of each, and of the herb of the white-thorn four measures, and boil them together and cover with white wine, and drink a dry draught every evening and every morning, and you shall recover; drink this first thing in the morning and last thing at night, for nine mornings to cleanse the stomach, then apply to the foot or hand a piece of fresh beef half an inch thick, and this will thoroughly heal you.

AGAINST TIGHTNESS OF CHEST AND HOARSENESS.

§ 81. Get a good quantity of the blessed oak and boil it in water until it runs off in drops, then strain it; and cast in the roots of the melot well shredded fine, and boil again, and use this warm at night and cold in the morning, keeping it in an earthen vessel.

AGAINST DANGER.

§ 82. Take the juice of rue, and cumin, and ground pepper, and boil together in honey, and make into a conserve, and use this night and morning, first thing in the morning and last thing at night.

AGAINST A MAN BEING BEWITCHED BY A WOMAN.

§ 83. Get the dung of a cock-horse and linseed, and temper them together, and boil into a poultice, and apply on a linen cloth to the wound, and use this plaster until it has drawn out all the burning fire from the wound, then apply the appropriate ointment to it, and it will be healed.

DISEASE OF THE CHEST.

§ 84. Get the roe of a salmon, and dry it slowly, and make it into a powder, and put it into ale to drink, and you will truly be healed.

PHYSICIANS OF MYDDVAI. 105

AGAINST DEAFNESS.

§ 85. Take twigs of elm wood, and place them on the embers, and receive the water that comes from the twigs in a clean vessel, and get the fat of a black eel, and as much honey, and as much juice of houseleek, mix them together, and put into the ear, and stop it with wool from the fleece of a black lamb, and it will truly be healed.

AGAINST VOMITING OF BLOOD.

§ 86. Get bean flour and honey, and egg yolks, and make a cake, and bake it on the hearthstone, with a pan and embers around the pan, and give some of the cake to the patient to eat frequently.

TO ESCAPE FROM ENEMIES.

§ 87. If one is going into a host, let him seek the blessed oak and place it in his clothing, and he will escape from his enemies.

TO MAKE AN OINTMENT.

§ 88. Take half a pound of pitch, and a quarter pound of wax, and half a pound of mutton fat, and powder of gall-stone, and boil them together, mixing all the while until they are combined, then put it in a box, or cast it in water and make it into a roll, and this will be good against every moist wound; spread it on linen or thin glove leather.

AGAINST THE STOPPAGE OF A WOMAN'S FLOWERS.

§ 89. Take rue and southernwood well, and press the juice in wine or strong ale, strain it and let it settle clear, and let the woman drink of it, and she will be healed.

TO CAUSE GOOD HEARING.

§ 90. Take young ash saplings of the size of twigs, and cut them, and place them on the trivet above the fire, and receive the drops that come from the ends, and take a spoonful of honey, and the tops of house-leek, and the heads and crooks of the leeks, and

106 PHYSICIANS OF MYDDVAI.

a little mustard pollen, and a shell full of eel grease, and boil everything together, stirring carefully the whole time while boiling, and put in a syringe lukewarm, and drive it into the ear on black wool, and it will heal.

FOR SWELLING OF A MAN'S PENIS.

§ 91. Get leaves of the ivy, and boil, and wash well, then get linseed leaves, and mallow, and boil in milk, and apply around the penis on fine linen.

ANOTHER.

§ 92. Roast eggs hard, and draw out the yolk and make into a fine powder, and make into an ointment, and press it through a linen cloth, and apply to the penis, and it is good against the great gout that may be in a bone, and against various other diseases.

ANOTHER.

§ 93. Get African fat and leeks, and apply as a plaster to the penis, and it will heal. You may use this plaster together with the medicine immediately preceding this, and that will be good.

A PLASTER AGAINST PROUD FLESH, AND TO DRAW OUT BAD FLESH.

§ 94. Take the bitter substance of the dunes and honey mixed with salt and vinegar, and mix well, and add a measure of rye flour, and boil, and make into a plaster, and apply to the wound, and use the plaster on a drink said to be good against the great gout until it heals.

FOR FEVER AND HOT SWELLING.

§ 95. Take two pennyworth of theriac, one pennyworth of saffron, and a little hart's horn ground very fine, and put over a good vial of drink, and mix well, and

PHYSICIANS OF MYDDVAI. 107

drink three mornings, then seek the red goose-grass of summer, leaves of sweet briar, and white bread of the cuckoo, and malt, and make them into a drink, and drink it three or four times a day in a dry swallow, and whoever does this will be healed.

GARTH DRINK.

§ 96. Take a pennyworth of antimony, and grind it fine as flour, and steep it for a day and a night in half a pint of sound ale, and strain it, and give it to the patient to drink on an empty stomach in the morning, then take a quart of posset and give it to him to drink over half an hour, three times, and after it has worked upon him, make a warm drink through spring water and put into it good butter and some honey, and drink it twice or three times, and he will be healed.

ANOTHER.

§ 97. Take the bark of the buckthorn, and press out the juice, and put two spoonfuls of it upon a dry swallow in a draught of good ale-broth, and drink it, and if it does not work, drink another swallow of the broth without the dregs of the gruel, and after it has worked, take as food warm oatmeal porridge made through spring water, with honey and butter in it, and wheaten bread therewith, and do this three times in nine days, and it will purge the body of all corrupt humours, and live after that for nine days on food of milk and wheaten bread therewith, and the warm water and flour mentioned, alternately.

ANOTHER.

§ 98. Take a handful of leaves of the damask rose and boil them in good ale-broth, and drink it, and follow the diet as already described for nine days.

ANOTHER.

§ 99. Take equal measures of the bark and juice of the buckthorn, and boil them together over a slow fire, and keep in a bottle

108 PHYSICIANS OF MYDDVAI.

glass tightly sealed, and when needed take two or three spoonfuls of it, and half an hour after swallowing it, drink a dry draught of good ale.

A REMEDY FOR A SORE MOUTH.

§ 100. Take a spoonful of the juice of cleavers, and a spoonful of elder juice, and two spoonfuls of the juice of unripe blackberries, and the pulp of a warm apple, and three spoonfuls of honey, and boil over a slow fire, stirring continuously until it becomes a thick electuary, put it in an earthen box and close it well to keep for use, and when the mouth is sore, take as much as a pigeon's egg will hold in your mouth until it dissolves, and it is good.

ANOTHER.

§ 101. Take elder leaves, and vine leaves, and cleavers, and rosemary, and briar leaves, and boil well in water and cover, then sweeten with honey, and wash your mouth by holding the liquid in your mouth as long as you can, then spit it out three times, after which swallow a dry draught of it, to cool the stomach.

ANOTHER.

§ 102. Take four spoonfuls of honey, and the juice of four oranges, and three spoonfuls of the juice of cleavers, and three of the juice of blackberries, and three of the juice of unripe blackberries, and boil over a slow fire until it becomes a thick electuary, and keep in a sealed box, and put as much as a pigeon's egg in your mouth, and hold it there until it is entirely dissolved.

FOR THE COLD PHLEGM-SICKNESS.

§ 103. Take half a pound of the juice of chickweed of the hedges, and a spoonful of honey in it, morning and night.

ANOTHER.

§ 104. Take half a pound of the juice of blackberries, and in it a spoonful of fresh honey, morning and night.

PHYSICIANS OF MYDDVAI. 109

AGAINST HOT URINARY DISEASE.

§ 105. Take the juice of hedge bindweed, the juice of watercress, the juice of wood sorrel, and the juice of elder, equal amounts of each, and drink half a pound of it morning and night for nine days, and live for another nine days entirely on a diet of milk and wheat bread, with no other food or drink; and it is good to take a purge two or three times before this medicine, to cleanse the body of the corrupt humour.

AGAINST THE HUMOUR THAT WEAKENS THE BODY AND THE MIND.

§ 106. Take the juice of apples, or the juice of raspberries, or the juice of plums, or the juice of blackberries, strained, and place on a gentle heat, adding a spoonful of honey for each swallow, and warm it gently; then drink a thirsty swallow morning and night for nine days, and take as food bread made from the flour of tall acorns, with no other food or drink during that time, and you will be well.
The best of all fruit juices, when in season, is the juice of the small sloe of the hedges and the juice of blackberries; and where there are no acorns, roast a handful of roots before the fire at a distance, grind them into flour, make bread of it, and you will live upon it.

ANOTHER.

§ 107. Take a spoonful of mustard seed three times a day, and wash it down with a swallow of good old mead, and live on a diet of cow's milk and fine wheat bread of tall grain, with small and frequent meals.

AN OINTMENT FOR KNEES, ANKLES, AND JOINTS.

§ 108. Take the plant called by some the herb of the joints, and sheep's or goat's tallow, and pound them together until they become an ointment; then place the ointment in a pan, and add to it a little honey and salt, and boil well on a gentle heat, and strain thoroughly, and with this anoint the pain, and you will be healed, by God's grace.

110 PHYSICIANS OF MYDDVAI.

TO DRAW OUT IRON OR THORNS, AND TO OPEN THE WOUND.

§ 109. Take nettle roots, and goose-fat and honey, pound them to a poultice, and apply to the wound, and it will silently open it and draw out whatever is in it.

AGAINST HEAT AND PAIN IN WOUNDS, WHICH WILL NOT LET THE PATIENT SLEEP.

§ 110. Take the bark of holly, and horehound, and the inner bark of elder, equal amounts of each, and add to them fat and wine in equal measure, and boil well until it is thick, then take a linen cloth, and spread the ointment on it, and place some of it on a warm compress, and lay it in the wound on the linen dressing, and place along with the compress a poultice of leeks on the wound, and it will heal by the grace of God.

A GOOD OINTMENT FOR TREATING WOUNDS.

§ 111. Take oil of olive, and if that is not available, boar's fat, and wine measure for measure, and boil well together, stirring constantly while boiling, and when it becomes thick put it in an earthen box, or in a bladder to keep, and close it up well, and wherever it is needed, anoint the wound with it.

AN OINTMENT AGAINST INFLAMMATION OF THE FLESH.

§ 112. Take good cow's cream and white wine, or strong apple juice, or old mead of some strength, and boil well together, equal measure of each until thick, stirring constantly, and when cool, put in a bladder or box to keep, and when needed, anoint the inflammation with it.

FOR COUGH AND HEART FAILURE.

§ 113. Take the root of parsley, and red fennel, and river bindweed, and pound them well, and take three-quarters of strong dark brose, and boil the essence of the herbs in it until the three-quarters reduces to one, then take the worth of

PHYSICIANS OF MYDDVAI. 111

sixpence worth of anise powder and sweeten it well like thick syrup, and boil it in that liquor, and put it to keep in a warm place, and this is called the stomach medicinal drink, and it will truly destroy the cough.

TO MAKE THICK HONEY.

§ 114. Take one measure of honey and four measures of spring water, and put them in a clean brass pot to boil, and when the wax and oil come to the surface, remove them with a basin until the boiling begins to froth, then boil over a moderate fire until the water has all evaporated and the honey remains thick in the pot, then take it and store it in an earthen vessel and close it well, and it will be the best of all honeys in medicines and foods.

OINTMENT FOR PAIN.

§ 115. Take the pulp of crab apples and boil them in wine until the wine is fully consumed, then mix this with wax, rosin, clear honey, and old lard, and boil well, and strain it clean, and anoint the painful area frequently, and it shall be healed through God.

TO CAUSE A WOMAN TO GIVE BIRTH SMOOTHLY AND QUICKLY.

§ 116. Take the juice of water-mint, or water-mint itself, having pounded it well with white wine, and strain it clean, and give it to her to drink. If a woman has a dead child lodged within her, let her drink this juice and the juice of alexanders, half and half, and it will free her through God.

FOR A BURN ON A PERSON'S FLESH FROM FIRE OR WATER.

§ 117. Take the roots of the lily and wash them clean, and boil them firmly in water, then mix them well with egg whites and oil, pellitory, or elm oil, and if that is not available, cream from good cow's milk or fresh unsalted butter, and apply it to the painful area, and the larger the poultice applied to it, the better.

112 PHYSICIANS OF MYDDVAI.

FOR SWELLING, AND HEAT, AND BRUISING, OR THE NATURE OF A COLD FROM EXERTION, AND ULCERS THAT ARE ON THE LEG, OR SINEWS, OR THIGH, HOWEVER GREAT THE INFLAMMATION, AND HOWEVER RED THE COLOUR, AND HOWEVER PUTRID THE FLESH AND THE WOUND, HAVING RESISTED MANY REMEDIES.

§ 118. Take white marl and grind it fine, and boil it in spring water that has had three heatings, and if any grease rises upon it, skim it finely until that is done, and keep it carefully, and a pennyworth of ointment in a quart of this water is sufficient; take a linen cloth and wash the wound frequently, and it will reduce the swelling, the heat, the inflammation, and the pain. Use this washing in that manner, and truly whatever wound it may be, whether cancer or a bruised ulcer, that water will heal it, but only from long use of anointing it by the fire. And when it is used up, make another, and a pennyworth of alum in a quart of water will be sufficient, and if you do thus you will be healed; it is proven.

FOR SUNBURN, OR ANOTHER HEAT ON THE FLESH.

§ 119. Take the juice of pennywort, and cream of milk in equal parts, and boil over a slow fire until it becomes a thick ointment, and keep it in a closed box.

FOR ITCHING OR THE ITCH.

§ 120. Take the root of elecampane, and boil it well in clean water after it has been washed clean, and when the root is soft, pound it well, then put thick cream from a cow's milk upon their tops, and mix into an ointment, and anoint your body with it before going to sleep once every three days, that is three times in nine days, and drink a gulp of the water in which the root was boiled three times a day for nine days, and you will be healed of the heat, and your body will be vigorous, for the water is good for healing and reviving the stomach and the lungs.

PHYSICIANS OF MYDDVAI. 113

AN OINTMENT AGAINST DISEASE OF THE LUNGS.

§ 121. Take the fat of a wether and honey, and boil them together, and when they have boiled enough, take nine pieces of fine wool, and dip them in the ointment and place each one separately to cool, and when they are cool, lay the nine upon the chest, covering the width from armpit to armpit, and from near the shoulder down toward the navel, and leave them on your chest for nine days; after that take away one of the wool pieces each day, until all nine are gone, and while this is being done, take as food wheaten bread throughout, with pure honey upon it as a sandwich in the morning, and the same bread with cow's milk at midday, and baked apples with goat's milk at night, and take between meals a good spoonful of pure honey, and you will be healed, by God.

ANOTHER AGAINST DISEASE OF THE LUNGS.

§ 122. Take hound's tongue, and pound it fine, and put clean water on it, and let it stand for three hours, then strain it hard through a fine sieve, and put it on a gentle fire to warm, with plenty of honey in it, and take half a swallow of it every three hours, and live on white wheaten bread and milk, and when you are thirsty take an apple and bake it, and put it in as much good old ale as will cover it, and eat the apple, and after an hour drink the ale, taking nothing else for food or drink.

ANOTHER.

§ 123. Take cow's milk, half a man's meal, and put into it two spoonfuls of pure honey, and take with it as food good wheaten bread three times a day, and between meals spoonfuls of hound's tongue juice, with a spoonful of honey mixed in.

And where you cannot obtain these herbs or any other herbs mentioned herein fresh enough to extract their juice, take the

114 PHYSICIANS OF MYDDVAI.

herbs dry, and boil them in a quantity sufficient to cover them in water in an iron pot until half has evaporated, then strain it hard through a fine cloth, and afterwards take half the measure of the boiling water of honey, and boil them together a second time until a third has evaporated, and keep it in a sealed glass bottle.

ANOTHER.

§ 124. Take as sole food white wheaten bread and honey, and as sole drink, the breast milk of a young healthy woman, for nine days without ceasing, then in place of breast milk, take goat's milk for nine more days, and continue this longer if there is need.

FOR SORENESS AND THE STONE.

§ 125. Take the milfoil and the stonecrop, and pound them in warm water, and give it as a drink to the patient for six days continuously, and let him drink no other drink, and he shall be healed, through God.

FOR SORENESS AND THE STONE.

§ 126. Take the blood of a hare and its skin, and make into a powder, and mix with the juice of crab apples, or with mead, or with whatever drink is taken, though the juice or the mead will be best, and let the patient drink that as his sole drink, and it will break the stone and expel it, and if you wish to prove this, take a spoonful of that powder in water, and place it in a hole that is in a limestone rock, and by the next morning it will have broken the stone, as is true.

FOR SORENESS AND OBSTRUCTION IN MAKING WATER.

§ 127. Take sea parsley, a herb similar in its leaves to the parsley that grows in gardens, with a roasted taste to it, and take rue, and saffron combs, and a quart of white wine, pound the

PHYSICIANS OF MYDDVAI. 115

Grind the herbs very fine, and boil them in wine until reduced by half, then strain cleanly through a fine sieve, and give the patient three doses, and he will truly be healed.

FOR PAIN AROUND THE HEART.

§ 128. Take the agrimony, pound it fine, and boil it in old ale, strain it clean, then boil until reduced by half, and take twice as much honey, boil them together a little, and take a vial of it fasting every morning until the ninth day, and it will draw out the pain and discomfort around the heart and stomach by truly taking it.

ANOTHER METHOD OF MAKING THE SAME MEDICINE.

§ 129. Take the agrimony, and boil it well in old ale, then take the herbs from the ale and pound them well in a mortar, and boil again well, and strain through a clean fine sieve, and take that juice with twice as much honey, boil a little, and use it taken fasting for nine mornings, and it will heal the pain and discomfort around the heart and in the stomach, through God.

A PRECIOUS OINTMENT AGAINST ALL KINDS OF PAIN.

§ 130. Take old lard, and goat tallow, and sheep tallow, and yellow wax, and take the bitters, and clay, and pound them well, and boil them through butter, then add the tallow, and the lard, and the wax, and boil well, and strain clean and firmly through linen, and keep this carefully, and it will cure every pain.

AN OINTMENT AGAINST ALL DISEASE THAT IS IN SINEWS AND VEINS.

§ 131. Take earthworm, and an onion top, make a hole, and put the worm in the hole, and place under the ashes to bake, and after that apply it to the pain, and leave it there for three nights without moving.

116 PHYSICIANS OF MYDDVAI.

AN OINTMENT FOR WHATEVER A PERSON MAY NEED IT.

§ 132. Take goose fat, cat's fat, the fat of a red boar, three heads of onion, and three measures of blue wax, the springs, and the bitter herb, and goosegrass, scarlet strawberry, and watercress, and boil them in spring water, and after boiling put them in a goose bladder, keeping it well away from the fire, and the ointment that comes from it should be kept carefully in a box, as a precious ointment for every pain in a person's body, as Hippocrates once made: it is proven.

AGAINST A FILM ON A PERSON'S EYE.

§ 133. Take the gall of a raven and mix it well with the white of an egg, and put a little in your eye, and take a little fine linen cloth and place it on the back of your eye, and do this morning and night, and truly you will be healed.

AGAINST A BRUISED ELBOW, OR KNEE, OR LEG.

§ 134. Take white fat — that is, lard rendered once — place it on a cloth or flannel against the swelling, and if it be on the knee or elbow, add the juice of rue to it, and it will heal the joint's wound and it will be healed; it is proven.

AGAINST SWELLING, AND HEAT, OR A BURNING OF A NATURAL KIND, OR ANOTHER WOUND.

§ 135. Take the bark of the elm tree and grind it fine, and remove the outer layer, and steep it in warm water until the water becomes like thick honey, and then draw the bark away from it, and take barley flour and fresh butter and boil it until it becomes a porridge, and apply it on a flannel poultice to the pain, and if it is thought that there is a broken bone within, add more bark to the plaster, and it will bring them to their place, as may truly be seen, if used frequently.

PHYSICIANS OF MYDDVAI. 117

FOR PAIN AND RINGING IN THE EAR.

§ 136. Take a loaf of wheaten bread fresh from the oven, split it into two halves, and apply to both ears as hot as can be endured, bind them and sweat thus, and you will truly be healed through God.

FOR HEARTBURN AND INFLAMMATION OF THE WET STOMACH.

§ 137. Take raisins of paradise, and a little powder of cloves among them, and eat for a week, and you will truly be healed through God.

TO BRING ON A WOMAN'S FLOWERS.

§ 138. Take hart's tongue, and boil in water briskly, and give lukewarm to drink, and she will be healed.

FOR PASSING BLOOD.

§ 139. Pound garlic and boil in milk in due season, and drink night and morning, and you will be healed.

FOR A WOMAN'S FLUX, AND FOR EXCESSIVE FLOWERS.

§ 140.
