Here is shown the weights and measures that every Physician should practice with, so that he may know firmly the amount required of every thing for its need and cause; namely,

Weight and measure of the Balance,
XX grains of wheat make one scruple.
3 scruples make one pennyweight.
4 pennyweights make an ounce.
12 ounces make a pint.
And thus let them be written in the books of the Physicians.
Grain thus: G
Scruple thus: D
Pennyweight thus: S
Ounce thus: Z
Pound thus: S

And thus are they distributed according to these letters, namely:

XX  G to D
3   D to S
4   S to Z
12  Z to S

The weight of liquid and wet things shall be distributed thus:—
Four spoonfuls make one spoonful [ladleful].
Four ladlefuls make one coccewy.
Four coccewy make one phialful.
Four phials make one pail, that is a quart.
Four quarts or pails make one gallon.
Four gallons make one tub.
Four tubs make one hogshead.
Four hogsheads make a mead-measure.
Four mead-measures make a mydd.
And thus are the measures of liquid and wet things distributed.
Here are other measures noted by the Physicians:—
Two coccewy, a half-pan.
Two half-pans, a pan.
Two pans, a phial.
Two phials, a cup.
Two cups, a bowl, that is a quart.

And all measures of weight, and all measures of liquid, ought to be warranted by weight and measure, for the sake of warranted and required knowledge, so that the medicine given to a patient be neither unfruitful nor poisonous, and so that every dose be of the amount that ought to be provided.

Here are approximate measures according to the understanding of the Physician:—
Four grains of wheat, a pea.
Four peas, an acorn.
Four acorns, a pigeon's egg.
Four pigeon's eggs, a hen's egg.
Four hen's eggs, a goose's egg.
Four goose's eggs, a swan's egg.

And no guarantee can be given on these quantities, except by the understanding of the Physician.

The four chief causes of disease and pain, which are bred in the body of man, are namely:—

i. Corruption, which comes from the effect of heat and cold.

ii. Infection in the blood or the humours, which comes from the improper use of food and drink.

iii. Obstruction in the stomach, or the veins, or other cavities of the body, so that the food, drink, blood, and humours cannot proceed in their proper course.

iv. Pestilence, that is plague or blight, which comes from poison entering the body. And from these four things all disease and pain in the body of man are bred, and by effective medicines they are cured.

These are things that are good to be known by every Physician, and every Head of Household, namely:

Berwyn: pouring boiling water or other liquid from a pool over the herbs or whatever the cause or necessity requires.
Isgell: boiling the herbs or other things in the water or other liquid from a pool as need and cause require.
Gwysg (also gwysgon): pouring boiling or cold water, or other liquid from a pool, as required, over herbs or other preparations, leaving to stand, and then straining through a press.
Mwyd: pouring cold or boiling water or other liquid from a pool over that which will soothe, to be mixed into a wet poultice to be applied.
Cyffaith: liquid ingredients mixed together, with syrups or other things that can be taken at a single swallow.
Edlyn: a draught, or a liquid made by art.

Ednyw: a vapor or steam, which is drawn in a breath through the mouth, or the nostrils, or the stomach, or the head, or the throat, or otherwise.
Cyflaith: a blending of ingredients into a paste taken by swallowing.
Cyfnyw (also cyfnywydd): the nature that exists within a man or other living creature, or a herb, or any other thing — that is, the virtue, or the faculty, or the nature that belongs to and resides in it.
Pelennau: medicinal ingredients properly prepared and made into small pills, to be taken at a single swallow.
Ennaint: an isgell or ointment into which a limb is placed, or which is applied to a limb.
Agolch: a lotion with which a pain is washed, hot or cold as required.
Cyfarpar: a specific diet of food and drink by the advice of a Physician.

These are the things that a Physician ought to have, and the qualities that ought to be in him, called the Necessaries of a Physician, namely:

i. A lancet for bleeding, for letting blood and opening a sore, and a knife somewhat larger.

ii. A spatula of steel or silver for spreading plasters and ointments.

iii. A syringe and a bladder, for injecting a liquid into the passage or the throat.

iv. His plasters, his ointments, his pills, his powders, and his draughts, kept by him, ready for need and occasion.

v. A garden of trees and herbs, kept as a nursery for the species of herbs, and shrubs, and trees, not to be found everywhere in the wild, and for maintaining exotic trees and herbs from countries that require shelter and care before they can thrive and be preserved in Wales.

PHYSICIANS OF MYDDVAI. 297

6. Also, he ought to have by him his herbs dried, and their roots, and their seeds, and their bark, kept carefully to hand, so that they may be obtained in winter, and at other times when they are not growing above ground.

7. Also, he ought to have carefully to hand his honey, his wax, his pitch, his storax, his rosin, his gums, his oils, his lard, his suet, his ointments, his minerals, his ale, his wine, his mead, his opiates, his distillations, and other things of need and purpose.

8. Also, he ought to have to hand his mortars, his strainer, his press, his earthen vessels, his glass vessels, his wooden vessels, his fire vessels, his storage vessels in glass, or in earthenware, or in silver, and with good lids upon them, so that the medicines be not rendered ineffectual, nor poison enter into them, nor he be poisoned through carelessness, and fault, and ignorance.

9. Also, he ought to have to hand his weights and his scales, in silver or in tin, lest poison enter into the medicine, and all his measures for liquid and dry in silver or in tin, with the same prudence, and also all his flesh-cutting instruments, lancets, and knives, and other cutting tools, and his cases.

10. All his weights, and his measures, both liquid and dry, ought to be warranted by standard measure and weight, so that he may know the quantities in every thing, lest they be too large or too small, for either of those would render the medicine ineffectual or poisonous.

11. He ought to have to hand his authoritative books of the art, and those approved by teachers, so that he may be able to judge and know the learning of the wise and skilled Physicians who came before him, and who wrote their books with authority in Welsh, in Latin, and in the Arabic tongue.

12. Also, he ought to be skilled in his art of medicine, as warranted in the judgment of the Wise, and Teachers, and the Learned of the art.

13. He ought to be a kind man, gentle, tender, generous, intelligent, wise, and gentlemanly, in achievement and in custom, and in word, and in conduct, and taking care not to shame one who is compelled to consult him, and above all in any place where he is obliged to question a girl or a woman.

14. He ought to be knowledgeable in all matters pertaining to his art of medicine, and able to read every sign and symptom of disease and pain, and to question the patient according to the nature of the pain, whether husband or wife, son or daughter, according to age, and constitution, and temperament, and to do all this in a most seemly manner, and with gentleness and courtesy in his conduct and his speech.

15. He ought to keep a secret firmly, and not reveal it for anything, or for any person, or for any consideration in the world.

298 PHYSICIANS OF MYDDVAI.

13. He ought to keep himself firmly from drunkenness, and frequenting taverns, and committing fornication disgracefully with a woman, for one cannot trust or rely upon a physician who does those evils, nor can the respect owed to learning and the arts of skill be given to him.

14. He ought to be a man sworn to his country and to foreign lands, against committing treachery and conspiracy from himself in his art against native or stranger, nor against kinsman nor enemy, for the office of a Physician is not to kill but to preserve from that which would kill, and to act according to the will of God and his peace, and not out of anger and enmity of one man toward his fellow.

15. He ought to carry with him, wherever he may go, his instruments of flesh, his remedies, and his means of relief, so that he may be able to help those who have need of him.

16. He ought to keep himself within reach of his home as much as possible, so that he may be found there when need of him arises.

17. He ought to be godly in his qualities and his customs, so that the grace of God may be upon him and upon what he does, and that there may be conscience in him to do what is right and beneficial in his art.

And these things are called the essentials of a Physician.

And thus ends this Book of Medicine, and I, Hywel the Physician, son of Rhys, son of Llewelyn, son of Philip the Physician, drew it out from the old authoritative books of the original Physicians of Myddvai, namely Rhiwallon the Physician and his three sons, no other than Cadwgan, and Gruffudd, and Einion, and the other Physicians of their children and descendants who came after them.

And I, Hywel the Physician, am descended line from line from forebears, from that Einion son of Rhiwallon the Physician of Myddvai, and I am living in Cilgwryd in Gower, and may there be from God grace and blessing upon this book, and upon whoever learns and acts according to it, for the sake of the knowledge of the art to please God, and to heal the sick and the wounded.

Amen. May it be so with God.

I, William Bona, copied this from the book of Sion Jones, Physician of Myddvai, who was the last of the lineage of the Physicians of Myddvai; Anno Christi, 1743.

And I, Iolo Morganwg, carefully copied it from the book of the above William Bona, now in the possession of Thomas Bona, Physician of the Parish of Llanfihangel Iorwerth, in the county of Carmarthen, in the month of the year 1801; and with the old Hywel the Physician I say,

May the grace of God be upon it. Amen.

THE

Physicians of Myddvai.

INTRODUCTION.
The following work is a book of remedies, which have been proved to be the best and most suitable for the human body, through the research and diligent study of Rhiwallon the Physician, and his three sons, Cadwgan, Griffith, and Einion, who were Physicians to Rhys Gryg, son of Griffith son of Rhys son of Tewdwr, their Lord, who granted them rank, lands, and privileges at Myddvai, for their support in the practice of their art and science, and for the healing and benefit of those who sought their help.
Here, therefore, with God's help, is set out the art of healing the injuries and diseases to which the human body is most prone, and the methods of managing them.
In the name of the Father, of the Son, and of the Holy Ghost. Amen, and so may it always be.

FLATULENT DYSPEPSIA.
§ 1. Take parsley seed, bruise it well, and boil it in the juice of the same plant. Let it be drunk warm while the pain is present.

ACUTE STOMACH PAIN.
§ 2. Take buckbean and grind it to a powder. Also, burn a quantity of gorse or broom seed in an iron pot and reduce it to a fine powder. Pour a gallon of strong old mead over the ingredients, then cover it well and boil it, and let it stand

302 PHYSICIANS OF MYDDVAI.

covered until cold. You should then drink as much of it as you need, night and morning on an empty stomach; at other times you should drink nothing but water until you have recovered your health.

ANOTHER.

§ 3. Drink a decoction of blessed thistle for nine mornings, and stop taking it for the nine mornings that follow, then drink and stop as before for nine mornings; and again in the same way for nine more mornings. Let your diet consist of wheaten bread and cow's milk.

AN EYE TREATMENT.

§ 4. Take half a pint of the best white wine, and an amount equal to a hen's egg of copper ore. Heat the ore in the fire until it is red hot, then quench it in the wine, repeating this process nine times. This liquid, placed in a well-covered glass vessel and kept covered for nine days, will be ready for use when needed; apply a drop or two to the eye morning and night. If wine cannot be obtained, strong old mead or old cider (which is the wine of apples) may be used instead.

TO BREAK AN ABSCESS.

§ 6. Take a small portion of the herb called rue, a portion of leavened bread, and half a spoonful of glue. Boil these ingredients in the sediment of old ale, mixing them well together until the mixture thickens; when needed, apply it hot to the abscess.

FOR TOOTHACHE.

§ 7. Take distilled water of red roses, a small portion of beeswax, and a little fresh butter, in roughly equal amounts. Mix the ingredients together in a dish over embers, then dip a linen cloth into the mixture and apply it to the affected jaw as hot as can be tolerated.

OINTMENT FOR AN ULCER.

§ 8. Take four portions of rosin, two of wax, one of lard, and four of verdigris; let these ingredients be boiled

PHYSICIANS OF MYDDVAI. 303

together on a slow fire, and strained through a coarse cloth. It should be kept in a well covered leaden vessel.

FOR ALL KINDS OF ACHES.
Section 9. Take linseed, boil it in milk, and apply to the painful part.

TO HEAL A WOUND.
Section 10. Take yellow wax, melt it on a slow fire, and take bruised cumin seed, mix with the molten wax, then stir these ingredients with a stirrer until cold. Apply this as a plaster to the wound.

ANOTHER METHOD.
Section 11. Take bruised linseed, the white of an egg, a small portion of sheep's cream, and a little honey, make them into a plaster and apply to the wound.

FOR A BURN OR A SCALD.
Section 12. Roast a dozen eggs until stone hard, then take out the yolks and put them in a frying pan, fry them until they become an ointment, and strain it; anoint the injured part with this, then take a bladder, spread mucilage of lime twigs on it, and apply to the injured part.

FOR HEMORRHOIDS.
Section 13. Take smoke-dried goat's flesh, dry it completely, and reduce it to as fine a powder as you can; lay some of it on live coals in a fireproof utensil, place this in a commode and sit over it.

AN OINTMENT TO PROMOTE THE REMOVAL OF DEAD TISSUE FROM AN ULCER.
Section 14. Take a spoonful of good vinegar, a spoonful of honey, a little verdigris, and the same quantity of aloes, boil together and keep ready for use.

A LOTION TO WASH AN INFLAMED PART.
Section 15. Take greater plantain, honeysuckle, and white roses, distil them together, and add some camphor to the product, letting it remain in this liquid continuously.

Section 17. Roast some crab apples, take some of the pulp and half as much honey; let this be the child's only food for a day and a night.

Section 20. Take the juice of celandine, drop it into the eye, and keep it closed for as long as it takes to count to a hundred. Let this treatment be diligently continued.

Section 21. Take wall pepper in small pieces, the dregs of small beer, wheat bran, and mutton suet; pound them well together in a mortar, then boil together over a slow fire and apply to the chest.

Section 39. Take eyebright and red fennel, a handful of each, and half a handful of rue; distil them, and wash your eyes with the liquid daily.

FOR SUPPRESSED MENSTRUATION.

§ 89. Obtain rue, pound it well, and press the juice into wine or strong ale, strain it and let it clear, then have the woman drink it, and she will recover.

TO IMPROVE HEARING.

§ 90. Obtain young ash shoots (about the size of rods), cut them, and lay them on a tripod over the fire, then collect the drops that will seep from the ends. Take a spoonful of honey, the tips of houseleeks, the heads and stalks of leeks, some mustard in flour, and a shell full of eel oil; boil all of these together, carefully stirring while they boil. Inject the mixture warm with a syringe into the ear, then stop the ear with the wool of a black lamb, and the patient will be cured.

A PLASTER FOR ERYSIPELAS AND THE REMOVAL OF PROUD FLESH.

§ 94. Take the juice of wood sage and honey mixed with salt and vinegar, mix the ingredients together well, then add a portion of rye meal and boil until a poultice can be formed from it. Use this poultice in conjunction with the drink recommended for gout, and the patient will soon recover.

FOR A FEVER OR INTENSE INTERMITTENT FEVER.

§ 95. Take two pennyworths of treacle, a pennyworth of saffron, and a little hartshorn grated fine, put them in a cupful of ale and mix well together, drinking it for three mornings; then obtain some sprigs of red raspberries, the leaves of sweetbrier, wood sorrel, and malt, make a drink from these, and take a hearty draught of it three or four times a day; whoever does this will recover.

316 PHYSICIANS OF MYDDVAI.

AN APERIENT DRINK.

Section 96. Take a pennyworth of stibium (Regulus of Antimony) and grate it as fine as flour, then mix it with half a pint of good ale, warm it, and let the patient drink it in the morning on an empty stomach. Afterwards obtain a quart of posset, and within half an hour let him drink it in three doses. When it has taken effect, make a warm drink with spring water, put some good butter and honey in it, then let the patient drink it two or three times and he will recover.

ANOTHER.

Section 97. Take the fruit of the buckthorn, press out the juice, and mix two spoonfuls of it with a full draught of good ale wort; let the patient drink it, and if it does not take effect let him drink another draught without the buckthorn. When it has taken effect, let him eat some warm oatmeal gruel made with spring water, mixed with some honey, butter, and unsifted wheaten bread. Let this be done three times over nine days and it will purge all corrupt humors from the body. After this course, let him live for a further nine days on milk-based foods and wheaten bread with the bran kept in, alternating with the warm water and flour drink previously mentioned.

ANOTHER.

Section 98. Take a handful of damask rose leaves, boil them in the wort of good ale, and drink it, following the diet described above for nine days.

ANOTHER.

Section 99. Take equal quantities of honey and the juice of buckthorn fruit, boil them together over a slow fire, and keep the mixture in a well-covered glass bottle. Take two or three spoonfuls when needed, and half an hour afterwards drink a hearty draught of strong ale wort.

A PREPARATION FOR A SORE MOUTH.

Section 100. Take a spoonful of sage juice, a spoonful of elder juice, two spoonfuls of cloudberry juice, the pulp of a hot apple, and three spoonfuls of honey, boil

on a slow fire, stirring continually until it becomes a thick confection. Keep it in an earthen pot, covering it well, so that it may be kept for use. When a case of sore mouth occurs, take an amount the size of a pigeon's egg and let it be held in the mouth until it dissolves, and it will be of benefit.

ANOTHER.

§ 101. Take elder leaves, honeysuckle leaves, sage, rosemary, and briers, boil well in just enough water to cover them, then sweeten with honey and wash your mouth with it, holding the liquid in your mouth as long as you can; then spit it out three times, and afterwards drink a generous draught of it to cool your stomach.

ANOTHER.

§ 102. Take four spoonfuls of honey, the juice of four oranges, three spoonfuls of the juice of sage, three of the juice of blackberries, and three of the juice of cloudberries, boil on a slow fire until it becomes a thick confection; keep in a covered pot, and place an amount the size of a pigeon's egg in your mouth, holding it there until it dissolves.

FOR A COLD HUMORAL CATARRH.

§ 103. Take half a pint of the juice of cleavers, with a spoonful of honey in it, morning and night.

ANOTHER.

§ 104. Take half a pint of blackberry juice, containing a spoonful of fresh honey, morning and night.

FOR AN INFLAMMATORY CATARRH.

§ 105. Take the juice of cleavers, the juice of watercress, the juice of sorrel, and the juice of elder, in equal parts; drink half a pint of this morning and night for nine days, and live the following nine days on a milk diet and wheaten bread, thoroughly ground; let no other food or drink be taken, and it will be advisable to take a laxative two or three times before starting this medicine, in order to clear the body of corrupt humors.

318 PHYSICIANS OF MYDDVAI.

FOR HUMORAL FLATULENCE, WEAKENING THE BODY AND MIND.

§ 106. Take the juice of apples, raspberries, plums, or blackberries, strained; place over a slow fire, adding a spoonful of honey for each serving, and bring to a gentle boil. Then drink a good, hearty amount of this each day for nine days. Eat only bread made from well-roasted acorns, and take no other food during this time, and you will recover.
The best fruit juice, when in season, is that of sloes and blackberries. When acorns cannot be obtained, dry nettle roots before the fire at a distance, grind them to powder, make bread from them, and live on that.

ANOTHER

§ 107. Take a spoonful of mustard seed three times a day, washing it down with good aged mead, and keep to a diet of milk and well-baked wheat bread. Let your meals be light and frequent.

AN OINTMENT FOR THE ANKLES AND JOINTS.
§ 108. Take the rhodri, or (as others call them) radishes, and the suet of sheep or goats, and pound them well together until they form an ointment. Then place the ointment in a pan, add a little honey and salt, and boil well over a slow fire, straining thoroughly. Use this to anoint the painful joint, and it will be cured with God's help.

TO EXTRACT IRON OR FRAGMENTS OF WOOD FROM A WOUND, AND TO OPEN IT.

§ 109. Take nettle roots, goose grease, and honey, pound them into a poultice and apply it to the wound. It will work to open the wound and draw out whatever is lodged within it.

FOR INFLAMMATORY WOUNDS THAT PREVENT THE PATIENT FROM SLEEPING.

§ 110. Take holly bark, mallow, and the inner bark of elder in equal quantities, then add lard and wine in the same proportions; boil well until it becomes

PHYSICIANS OF MYDDVAI. 319

thick, then take a cloth and spread the ointment on it, and spread some warm on a dressing as well; insert this in the wound, and cover it over with the anointed cloth; apply some powdery ointment on the wound with the dressing, and with God's help it will be healed.

A GOOD HEALING SALVE FOR WOUNDS.
§ 111. Take olive oil, or, if none can be obtained, some lard and wine, in equal quantities, boil together well, stirring continuously while boiling; when it has thickened, keep it in an earthen vessel or bladder, covering it well. When needed, anoint the wound with it.

AN OINTMENT FOR EXTERNAL INFLAMMATION.
§ 112. Take cream from cows, and white wine or strong apple cider, or else well-aged mead; boil well together (in equal quantities of each) until it becomes thick, stirring continuously; when cold, keep in a bladder or box, and when needed anoint the affected area with it.

FOR BRONCHITIS WITH BREATHLESSNESS.
§ 113. Take the roots of parsley, red fennel, and river startip, and pound them well; take three quarts of strong dark ale and boil the appropriate amount of the herbs in it until the three quarts are reduced to one; then take six pennyworth of powdered anise, and enough clarified honey to sweeten it well, and boil in the above liquid, then set aside to keep in a warm place; this is called an expectorant medicine and will certainly cure the cough.

TO PREPARE CLARIFIED HONEY.
§ 114. Take one part honey and four parts spring water, and put in a clean brass pot to boil; when the wax and other impurities rise to the surface, remove them with a bassel* until it stops producing scum, then boil over a moderate heat until the water is completely evaporated, leaving the honey clarified in the pot; then put it in an

A PAIN-RELIEVING OINTMENT.
Section 115. Take the pulp of crabs and boil it in wine until the wine has completely evaporated, then mix in rosin, clear honey, and old lard, boil well and strain. Anoint the painful area with this ointment frequently, and with God's help the pain will be removed.

FOR A BURN OR SCALD.
Section 117. Take the roots of the lily, wash them clean and boil briskly in water, then mix them thoroughly with egg whites, petroleum ointment, or ointment of lime twigs — or if the last cannot be obtained, good cow's cream or fresh unsalted butter. Apply this to the burn; the more applied, the better.

FOR A SWELLING, HEAT, OR SPRAIN,
A CHILL AFTER A JOURNEY, OR FOR ERYSIPELAS OF THE LOWER EXTREMITIES — HOWEVER GREAT THE PAIN, REDNESS, OR INFECTED CONDITION OF THE DISEASED PART, EVEN IF MANY OTHER MEDICINES HAVE FAILED, THIS WILL HEAL IT.

Section 118. Take white alum, reduce it to powder, then mix it with spring water and bring it to three boilings. If any scum appears, remove it carefully until none remains, then store it with great care. A pennyworth of this solution in a quart of water will be sufficient to make a lotion, which should be applied frequently to the diseased area with a linen cloth. It will reduce the swelling, heat, redness, and pain. Indeed, if you continue to wash the area in this way, any disease — even spreading ulcers or gangrenous erysipelas — will be cured by this water, applied persistently by a fire. When the supply is used up, make more, and note that a pennyworth of alum in a quart of water is sufficient. Do this and you will be cured. This is proven.

FOR SUNBURN OR A SIMILAR EFFECT FROM ANY OTHER HEAT.
Section 119. Take marsh pennywort and cream in equal parts, and boil on a slow fire until it becomes a thick ointment. Keep it in a covered box.

PHYSICIANS OF MYDDVAI. 323

through a fine cloth, and give it to the patient at three draughts, and he will certainly be cured.

FOR A PAIN IN THE CARDIAC REGION.

§ 128. Take centaury, pound it well, boil in old ale and strain well, then boil down to half, take that with twice as much honey, and boil moderately; take a cupful of this on an empty stomach for nine days, and it will remove the pain and oppression from the region of the heart without fail.

ANOTHER WAY OF PREPARING THE SAME MEDICINE.

§ 129. Take centaury, boil it well in old ale, then remove the herbs from the ale, and pound them well in a mortar, boil again well, and strain through a fine cloth; take this juice mixed with twice the quantity of honey, boil moderately and make a habit of taking it on an empty stomach for nine days, and with God's help it will heal the oppression and pain around the heart.

A VALUABLE OINTMENT FOR ALL KINDS OF ACHES.

§ 130. Take old lard, the suet of a he-goat and a sheep, yellow wax, wormwood and primrose, bruise in a mortar, boil in butter, then add the suet, lard, and wax, boil well and press strongly through cloth, keep it carefully and it will ease all sorts of aches.

AN OINTMENT FOR ALL NERVOUS DISORDERS.

§ 131. Take earthworms and the bulb of an onion, make a hole in the onion and put the earthworms inside, then light a fire underneath to roast them; after that apply to the affected part, leaving it there for three nights without removing.

AN OINTMENT FOR GENERAL USE.

§ 132. Take a gander's fat, the fat of a male cat, a red boar's fat, three drams of blue wax (that is, copper-treated wax), watercress, wormwood, the red strawberry plant and primrose, boil them in pure spring water, and when boiled, stuff a gander with them and roast it at a distance from the fire; the grease that comes from it should be carefully kept in a pot. It is a

This is a valuable ointment for all kinds of aches in the human body, similar to one formerly made by Hippocrates. It is proven effective.

FOR AN OPACITY IN A MAN'S EYE.

§ 133. Take a rook's gall and mix it well with the white of an egg, place it in your eye, and lay a little fine linen over it. Do this morning and night, and you will surely be cured.

FOR AN INJURY IN THE ELBOW, KNEE, OR LEGS.

§ 134. Take lard, or pig's fat once melted, spread it on a cloth or flannel, and apply it to the swellings. If treating the elbow or knee, mix in some juice of rue, and it will cure an injury of the joint. This is proven.

FOR A SWELLING, AND HEAT, OR INFLAMMATION OF AN ERYSIPELATOUS NATURE, OR ANY OTHER KIND.

§ 135. Take elm bark and bruise it well, removing the outer skin, boil it down to the thickness of honey, remove the bark, and add barley meal and unsalted butter, boiling it into a poultice. Lay this on a flannel and apply it to the affected area. If a fragment of bone is suspected within, use a large quantity of bark in the poultice, and it will bring the fragment into union with the adjoining bone, if applied with perseverance.

FOR PAIN AND NOISE IN THE EAR.

§ 136. Take a loaf of wheaten bread (ground through) fresh and hot from the oven, divide it in two, and apply both halves to the ears as hot as can be tolerated, bind them in place, thus producing perspiration, and by the help of God you will be cured.

FOR CARDIALGIA IN A MOIST STOMACH.

§ 137. Take grains of paradise and powdered cloves, eat them for a week, and by God's aid you will be cured.

A PLASTER TO REDUCE A SWELLING.

§ 141. Take tutsan, cinquefoil, vervain, mallows, lard, and butter; boil the herbs well in water, then remove and pound them thoroughly, setting them back on the fire in the water a second time with butter and lard, mix and boil until it forms a poultice, and apply it to the swelling. It will reduce it without fail.

PHYSICIANS OF MYDDVAI. 325

FOR JAUNDICE.

Section 145. Take the leaves that grow on the branches of the hawthorn and mistletoe, boil them in white wine or good aged ale until the liquid is reduced by half, then remove from the fire and strain. Drink this three times a day and you will be cured.

A DRINK FOR STIFFNESS OF STOMACH AND BODY.

Section 147. Take a handful of rosemary, a handful of hyssop, a handful of sage, a handful of feverfew, and a handful of red fennel. Pound them well and boil in a gallon of good strong wort made from barley malt. Keep it in an earthen vessel, cover it carefully, and set it aside for three days. Then take three draughts of it while fasting each morning, and another draft at night warmed to body temperature. Also take a pennyworth of grains of paradise, a pennyworth of saffron, and a pennyworth of cinnamon bark powdered fine in a mortar, and sprinkle a portion on the surface of the drink, continuing to do this as long as the drink lasts. This has been proven valuable for all pains in a man's body.

FOR PNEUMONIA.

Section 148. Take a quantity of sea beet (called in Latin beta), discarding the branches and tops, and take three gallons of pure water and boil the beet in it. Then remove the beet, let the liquid continue boiling, and after a while remove it from the fire. Let it cool to the temperature of wort, then pour it onto some fresh ale sediment, allowing it to ferment as long as it will. Then give it to the patient as his only drink for nine meals. Then take the beet and mix it with butter and powdered melilot, giving it to the patient to eat for nine meals, and with God's help he will recover. It is also an excellent medicine for recurring fever.

FOR A FEVER.

Section 149. Take a handful of water iris, three quarts of good strong ale, pound the herbs, and boil in the ale until it is reduced to three quarts, then strain. Then take a pennyworth of powdered grains of paradise and boil briefly a second time. Take it four times a day before the fever episode comes on, and you will recover.

326 PHYSICIANS OF MYDDVAI.

FOR THE INTERNAL PAIN CALLED STONE.

§ 150. Take the herb called butterwort, which grows in meadows and on mountains, its leaves spreading close to the earth and bearing a blue, sparse flower. Gather a hood-full of these herbs and pound them well in a large wooden milk pail. Then take twice as much watercress and pound that briskly. Next, take a red cockerel, kill it, pluck it, gut it, and clean it well. Put it in a brass pot with at least two gallons of pure water and boil it together with the herbs until the bones loosen, at which point they should be removed. Return the flesh to the pot along with the herbs and boil briskly a second time until the mixture thickens and stops bubbling due to its thickness. Now take it off the fire and strain everything through a strong cloth. Put the strained liquid back on the fire, then add a half-pennyworth of powdered pepper, stir it in, and remove from the fire to cool, stirring throughout. Give some of this to the patient with his food and drink at each meal, until the diseased matter is found to be passing from him in a dissolved state. I have proved this to be effective for people of all ages. It is called "The blue confection for the Stone."

WHEN A MAN IS SWOLLEN FROM THE POISON OF A SPIDER.

§ 151. Take nine cloves of garlic, peel them carefully, add a spoonful of treacle and a quart of strong fresh ale, mix these together and give them to the patient to drink freely. At the same time, cover him with plenty of clothing so that he sweats well. If he can remain in this state for an hour he will recover, even if his skin had already become mottled. This remedy is also useful for a person bitten by an adder.

FOR SWELLING AND PAIN IN THE SHOULDERS, OR THE JAWS, AND UNDER THE EARS.

§ 152. Take celandine, the roots of red fennel, the heads of leeks, red wine and butter, pound them together

and apply them cold as a plaster to the part, and you will truly recover by the help of God.

FOR SCABS AND ERUPTIONS ON A MAN'S FLESH.

§ 153. Take celandine, the root of elecampane, and wood sorrel, boil them in as much water as you like until it is reduced by half, wash the diseased part with this liquid and it will be healed.

FOR PAIN IN THE BACK.

§ 154. Bleed from the back of the foot near the big toe, and bandage the limb after bathing it in warm water, and the patient will surely recover.

FOR A PAINFUL ERYSIPELAS IN THE LEGS AND LIMBS.

§ 155. Take the herb called buckthorn plantain and boil it in three gallons of water until it is reduced to a quart. Bottle it, then add a gallon of ale and boil again until reduced to a bottle, finally straining it. Keep it in a clean vessel and anoint the painful part with it frequently.

FOR DIFFICULTY URINATING AND THE ASSOCIATED PAIN.

§ 156. Take saxifrage and parsley, pound them well together, and boil with honey in old ale, then strain. Drink this morning and night and you will be cured, in the name of God.

FOR ULCERATION OF THE EARS.

§ 157. Take the seed of the ash tree, otherwise called ash keys, and boil them briskly in the urine of the sick person. Apply this to the ear as a warm compress and place some of it inside on black wool. By God's help it will cure it.

FOR JAUNDICE.

§ 158. Take the largest apple you can find and scoop out the core using a bone or wooden scoop, fill the cavity with the juice of white ox-eye (called by some the great daisy) and saffron, then replace the plug of apple, and bake the apple under the embers. When sufficiently baked, remove it from the embers and pound it thoroughly. Let the patient eat it and he will certainly recover.

328 PHYSICIANS OF MYDDVAI.

FOR A CHRONIC GASTROCELE.

§ 159. Take the bark of the blackthorn, scrape off the outer skin, and boil the inner bark in water for as long as it takes to boil beef. Afterwards, hard-boil an egg and take the yolk with fine wheat flour, mixing them well together. Then take one third of the liquid in which the bark was boiled, combine it with the meal and yolk mixture, make it into bread, and bake it on the hearthstone. This bread should be eaten morning and night. The patient should carefully avoid drinking anything other than the blackthorn liquid or red wine, and he will recover. — Philip the Physician.

FOR FAINTINGS OF THE HEART.

§ 160. Take equal measures of fennel juice and honey, boil them well together, and eat an amount equal in size to a hen's egg morning and night, and you will recover.

FOR HARDNESS OF THE ABDOMEN.

§ 161. Take two spoonfuls of holly juice, drinking it three times a day for nine days, and with God's help you will recover.

FOR A MOIST STOMACH.

§ 162. Take the roots of leeks and turn them into powder by drying them slowly at a distance from the fire, then grinding them in a mortar. Take a spoonful of this powder in a generous drink of red wine, and take it as the last thing at night, two hours after supper, for three days. With God's help you will recover.

FOR PNEUMONIA.

§ 163. Take the three following herbs — mugwort, tansy, and red fennel — a handful of each. Pound them well and make them into a potion with good, sound, aged ale. Boil on a slow fire, strain carefully, and drink cold over three meals. With God's aid this will remove the pain beneath the chest muscle and shoulder, curing the patient.

Another method of preparation is to pound the herbs well and pour three cupfuls of ale or old mead over them. Leave them to stand and cool for half an hour, then strain well

through a clean cloth, giving it in three portions to the patient once every three hours, and by God's help he will recover.

AN OINTMENT FOR ALL SORTS OF PAINS.

§ 164. Take broom flowers, or when they are unavailable, the branches and leaves, primroses, the roots of water hemlock, the leaves of sea holly, mugwort, and red dock; pound them well in a mortar and make an ointment using butter. Anoint the affected area frequently and it will be cured.

FOR DISORDER OF THE LIVER.

§ 165. Take a little wild tansy, pound it well with wine, strain it, and then drink it three times a day for three days, and by God's help you will recover. When no wine is available, take strong, sound ale or mead instead.

Borage will remove the reddish color from the bowel evacuations if it is pounded with wine and drunk. It will strengthen a person's memory and intellect, being truly a warm astringent tonic.

TO RESTRAIN THIRST IN A HEALTHY OR SICK PERSON.

§ 166. Take centaury and pound it with warm water, then strain it; when cold, let it be drunk, and it will relieve stomach pains and cure the patient.

FOR PAIN IN THE FEET AND SWELLING IN THE LEGS.

§ 167. Take the roots of the dwarf elder, remove the bark, boil them well, then pound them in a mortar with old lard, and apply as a poultice to the affected area.

FOR CLOUDING OF THE CORNEA.

§ 168. Take the leaves of the red garden strawberry and pound them with a hen's fat and unsalted butter; anoint your eye with this ointment when you go to sleep, so that it may penetrate into your eye, and you will recover.

ANOTHER REMEDY.

§ 169. Take a hen's fat, unsalted butter, and powdered aloes; boil them together and let them cool, then anoint your eyes when you go to sleep.

FOR STRANGURY.

§ 170. Take the juice of leek, honey, powdered pepper, and vinegar, pound them together well until fully combined, and give to the patient in three doses; this will cure him.

FOR DYSPEPSIA, STRANGURY, AND PAIN IN THE PERINEUM.

§ 171. Take two handfuls of tansy and pound them in a mortar, then boil them in spring water for as long as it takes to cook beef, until they form a thick mass. Sprinkle some barley meal on the surface, mix well, and spread onto a cloth or flannel. Apply this poultice to the painful area frequently, repeating up to nine times. Afterwards, take two quarts of perry and a quart of the blessed water of Rulandus (or emetic water), add some to wine as warm as the patient can tolerate, and have him drink it morning and night. Do not let him take the warm drink first and the emetic water after. He should follow this regimen for as long as the liquid lasts. While undergoing this treatment, obtain some ram's flesh, boil it well in spring water, then remove from the fire, take out the meat, and let the water cool. Skim off the surface fat, form it into a ball and melt it down, then boil this tallow with some of the blessed water over a low fire until it becomes an ointment, keeping the vessel well covered throughout. Rub the affected area back and forth with this ointment. Eat only oven-baked or griddle-baked bread and ram's flesh, and take no other food for a long time; by persisting in this plan you will recover, as has been thoroughly proven.

TO HEAL A BURN, EVEN WHEN IT INVOLVES THE JOINTS OR VEINS.

§ 174. Take groundsel, tutsan, and old lard, pound them well in a mortar and apply to the inflamed organ as a softening agent first. TO DESTROY PARASITES ON THE HUMAN BODY.

§ 175. Take rue, pound it well, wrap it up in a cloth, and rub the skin vigorously with it — this will destroy the parasites. It is also excellent for those exhausting sweats that so weaken a person.

FOR ANY KIND OF WOUNDED SKIN.

§ 176. Take feverfew, bruisewort, ribwort plantain, common plantain, and sage in equal portions, bruise them briskly in a mortar, and boil in unsalted butter until the butter is fully absorbed, then strain well and keep in a box. Anoint any bruised skin with this.

THE FOLLOWING IS A POTENT OINTMENT FOR DRAWING EVIL HUMORS FROM WOUNDS.

§ 177. Take feverfew, mugwort, devil's bit, plantain, and mallows, pound them well and add some unsalted butter, fresh yellow wax, rosin, and suet. Boil well, and the properties of the herbs will be transferred to the butter, suet, wax, and rosin. Strain through a cloth and keep in a box. It will draw out the poison from all kinds of wounds and heal them.

Neither food nor drink should be given to such patients, except sweet milk and breast milk.

FOR WORMS IN THE STOMACH.

§ 178. Make a powder of turnips by slicing and roasting them in front of a fire. They should be ground up and given to the patient to eat cold, for nine consecutive mornings on an empty stomach, or at nine separate times, and he will be cured.

FOR THE BITE OF AN ADDER.

§ 179. Take the juice of plantain, of ground ivy, and olive oil, in equal quantities. Give the patient a good drink of this, and anoint the wound with the same mixture. It will neutralize the poison and cure the patient.

ANOTHER REMEDY FOR AN ADDER'S BITE.

§ 180. Take the brain of a red rooster and the juice of the fern known as hart's tongue, pound them well and mix thoroughly with white wine or milk. Let the patient drink a full draught of this, and wash the wound with it as well, and he will be healed.

FOR A FRECKLED FACE.

§ 181. Anoint the face with the blood of a bull or a hare.

FOR SWELLING IN A MAN'S JOINTS OR LIMBS.

§ 182. Take centaury, pound it well, and strain it with water through a clean linen cloth. Let the patient drink it.

FOR EXCESSIVE THIRST.

§ 183. Take centaury and a small amount of bastard pellitory, pound them well, and press the juice into a strong barley malt wort, or let the herbs steep in the wort in an earthen vessel until the next morning. Given to the patient to drink in the morning, this will relieve his thirst.

FOR AN INTERNAL SWELLING.

§ 184. Take plums, boil them in goat's milk, and when cooled, let the patient drink it in the morning and as late in the evening as possible.

FOR RINGWORM.

§ 313. Take a handful of nettles, place them in a cloth against your nostrils, and plug your nostrils with some of the same. It is effective.

ERYSIPELAS.
Erysipelas has various forms, both hot and cold. The hot form is the more dangerous of the two and is accompanied by more extensive inflammation, the cold form being less so. Because of this they must be treated differently, the hot requiring cold remedies and the cold requiring hot ones. The cold form is treated as follows: this disease being (lanoole?) take the whites of eggs and rye meal, make a dough of them and leave it on the affected area until it falls away by itself. Repeat this until the area is healed.

A REMEDY FOR PUTRID FLESH, WITH LOCAL INFLAMMATION IN AND AROUND THE ULCERS.

§ 613. Take fine rye meal and clear honey, make a dough of them and apply to the ulceration. When necessary, renew the application, and this will restore the patient to health and activity.

A GENERAL REMEDY FOR ALL KINDS OF ERYSIPELAS.

§ 614. Take tow and cut it fine, wash it in the sediment from wheat ale, boil it well and apply to the affected area for a night and half a day. Then remove it and wash the area with male urine. Afterwards cover it with a powder prepared as follows: take some goose wings, pluck off the feathers, burn them to ash, powder them and apply to the disease. This should then be covered with the fat of a wildcat or pig's lard and a cabbage leaf. Then get some good old ale made with wheat unmixed with barley, fill a pitcher with it, add salt, arfemeint and pitch in equal parts, with more beeswax than any of the others. Boil them until they become thick, then remove from the fire and let it cool.

If your hearing is poor, dip some black wool into it and put it in your ears at night before bed.

Section 749. Take mugwort, plantain, and red nettle. Boil them in goat's whey, strain through linen, and give the liquid to the patient.

Section 750. Take water pimpernel, plantain, and fennel in equal parts. Pound them together with rye meal, honey, and egg whites. Apply this as a plaster and the swelling will heal.

Section 751. Take the juice of celandine and pound the herb well with breast milk from a mother nursing a male child, or with the urine of a one-year-old child. Strain through a press and apply the juice to your eye using a feather.

FOR OPPRESSION OF THE HEART.

§ 767. Take the juice of fennel and honey; boil together until they become firm, and eat a portion of it first thing in the morning before eating, and last thing in the evening after eating. It will cure you with God's help.

TO PREPARE A GARGLE.

§ 768. Take rosemary, sage, hyssop, alum, and good ale; put on the fire and boil until a quart is reduced to a pint. Once boiled, use it warm, and do so daily for a week.

The following are the virtues and properties of various medicinal herbs useful to man.

THE VIRTUES OF SAGE.

§ 785. Sage is useful when boiled to strengthen the nerves. If an infusion sweetened with honey is drunk, it is good for the lungs. If the fetus in the womb is dead, let the woman boil sage with white wine, strain it carefully, and she will be safely delivered without risk to her life. Also pound this herb and apply it to a poisoned wound, and it will draw out the venom; even if the wound is full of infection, it will be cleansed to the very bottom if dressed with this herb. Take some sage, pound it fine, and mix the juice with white wine, or steep the pounded herb in white wine, fresh wort, or old mead overnight and strain it, then drink it on an empty stomach. With God's help it will cure the patient. It is beneficial for healthy people to drink half a measure of this preparation in the morning on an empty stomach, in order to maintain good health and prolong life.

438 PHYSICIANS OF MYDDVAI.

THE VIRTUE OF THE IRIS.

§ 786. The iris is a herb with a white flower, and its virtues are these: its juice, mixed with honey and wine, will dissolve urinary stones. It will also cure fever and jaundice, as well as nervousness. When you have no wine, take the juice in strong sound mead, or strong malt wort. It is hot and dry in nature.

THE FOLLOWING ARE THE VIRTUES OF THE NETTLE.

§ 787. Take the juice of this herb mixed with white wine, strain it carefully, and let it cool. Drink some of it morning and night; it will cure jaundice, restore the blood, and remove any disease present in it. If the juice is taken mixed half and half with barley wort, it will cure pleurisy in the side, and will restore and invigorate an elderly man in both body and mind. If nettle seed in powdered form is taken mixed with wine, it is very useful for wind colic, difficulty urinating, or a chronic cough, and will reduce swelling, promoting a flow of urine without harming the bladder.

THESE ARE THE VIRTUES OF THE BETONY.

§ 788. Anyone who makes a habit of drinking the juice will avoid difficulty urinating. If it is boiled in white wine and drunk, it will cure colic and stomach swelling. Crushing it fine, pressing out the juice, and applying it with a feather to a person's eye will clear and strengthen sight and remove specks from the eye. The juice is good to drop into the ears of those who are deaf. The powder mixed with honey is useful for those who cough; it will relieve the cough and help with many diseases of the lungs. It is good for fever when it strikes, and if taken when there is no fever, it will prevent an attack for that entire year. If boiled with leek seed, it will cure the eye and both brighten and strengthen sight. A wise man has said that if reduced to powder, a snake would rather be broken to pieces than pass through it. Should there be swelling in the stomach, it will reduce it if boiled with wine and figs and then given to the patient in bed. It is a good thing

PHYSICIANS OF MYDDVAI. 439

to mix it with the juice of red fennel, and clear honey, for it will certainly clear the eyes, curing them if diseased, and strengthening the five senses wonderfully.

THE FOLLOWING ARE THE VIRTUES OF PARSLEY, CALLED PETROSILWM (PETROSELINUM) IN LATIN.

§ 789. Parsley is a good herb of a warm, hot nature, and moist in the third degree. It is useful in all food as a generator of blood. It will remove obstructions of the veins and arteries in a man's body, so that the humors may circulate properly as they should, and this it will certainly do.

It is also beneficial to use parsley for the relief of fainting, tertian ague, pleurisy, and dropsy, the juice being taken for three days in succession, without any other drink. It will greatly stimulate the spirits and strengthen the stomach.

There is a kind of parsley called in Welsh perllys yr hel, because it grows in places that are occasionally flooded by the tide, and is of a salty nature. In Latin it is called petroselinum marinum, and is good for all obstructions of the urine and humors of the body, as well as for colic and difficulty urinating, the juice being taken. The juice is also useful for destroying unhealthy tissue growth in a wound. It will grow in gardens, and should be cultivated wherever the sea is far away.

THE VIRTUES OF FENNEL, CALLED FUNICULWM (FUNICULUM) IN LATIN.

§ 790. Fennel is warm and dry in the second degree, and is useful for diseases of the eye. It is good against every kind of poison in a man's body, when drunk in the form of powder mixed with white wine or strong aged mead. It is useful for tertian ague and inflammatory fever. If the seed or herb is boiled in water until it is well infused with the plant's properties, and the head — when suffering from headache — is washed with it, it will greatly help and cure the condition, whether the headache is caused by cold or fever. It will remove the headache very quickly.

* Petroselinum. † Funiculum.

440 PHYSICIANS OF MYDDVAI.

THE FOLLOWING ARE THE VIRTUES OF ROSEMARY, CALLED YSBWYNWYDD, AND ROSA MARINA* IN LATIN.

§ 791. Rosemary is warm and dry in the third degree, and it is called a shrub because it falls between a herb and a tree.

Take the flowers of rosemary, mix them with honey, and eat them every day on an empty stomach. You will not suffer from nausea or any other harmful condition for as long as you use this remedy.

The flowers are also especially useful when boiled with honey or white wine reduced by half, and carefully strained. A spoonful or two should be drunk cold in the morning, with a little honey taken alongside. A small amount taken when one is struck by colic will relieve it within three hours. If you wish to apply it externally to your stomach, no honey should be added.

Take also the leaves of rosemary and wood sage, make them into a potion, and add honey in the same way. This is an excellent remedy for difficulty urinating, kidney stones, and catarrh. It will break down and expel these conditions through the urine.

Also, place their flowers or leaves under your head in bed, and you will not be troubled by unpleasant dreams or burdened by anxiety of mind.

Also, if you carry a stick or piece of this shrub, no evil spirit can come near you, nor can anyone do you any harm. Rosemary has all the virtues of the stone called jet.

Also, if you obtain a spoon made from the trunk or root of this shrub and drink broth with it during the day, you will be protected from poison, and you will be kept safe that entire day from thunder and lightning, as well as all harmful attacks.

Also, gather the leaves of rosemary, pound them fine, strain them, and drink the juice. It will remove all phlegm from the head and lungs, and cure it with complete certainty.

Also, if a man suffers from a urinary obstruction, let him obtain the flowers or leaves, boil them in white wine, and drink it as a potion — first thing in the morning and last thing at night.

* Rosa Maria.

Also, if the flowers are put with white wine in a distillery and distilled, the product will be equal to spirits of wine and will prove a suitable substitute in all cases. It is useful as a lotion for the head when affected with a headache from cold or fever, or when a man is threatened with insanity. A spoonful of this liquid with a spoonful of honey, and a spoonful of melted butter or thick fresh cream, is useful for a cough or the expulsion of phlegm from the lungs.

Also, a decoction of it is helpful to an insane person, or one threatened with delirium; indeed it is good for every disorder that can exist in the human body.

It is also beneficial to boil the flowers and leaves in water and to wash yourself well with it every morning, leaving it to dry naturally rather than with a cloth. By washing in this way consistently, the elderly will retain a youthful appearance for as long as they live. This water will expel phlegm from the brain and prevent griping when using purgatives. It will expel dropsy, cure the liver, bring warmth to the nerves and veins, disperse an abscess, lift the spirits, strengthen the bones, and increase the quantity and improve the quality of the marrow within them. It improves eyesight and relieves loose bowels when boiled in vinegar and applied to the stomach of the patient. It will promote the formation of blood and cure tertian fever. Should a man have weakened himself through sexual excess, he will be restored to his usual strength if he confines himself to this as his only drink for nine days.

It will also cure impotence in either sex if taken with food. When a couple are childless, let the wife, if young, use rosemary.

Also, if a man has a cold accompanied by fever, let him take rosemary, burn it, and inhale the smoke through his nostrils. It will cure him completely.

Let him also take the water in which the flowers and leaves have been boiled, adding a little honey and pepper, and drink it warm. It is useful for all kinds of coughs; this is true. Also, take the roots of the shrub, roast

them till they become a powder, then put [Welsh text] in truth.

The bark is useful for intolerable skin irritation, caused by a deteriorated condition of the blood.

Its root, also boiled in vinegar, is good for fomenting painful joints. Also rosemary and betony pounded and mixed with pure water is a good wash for all venomous bites, whether from animals or reptiles. It will cure them without the need for any other ointment.

THE FOLLOWING ARE THE VIRTUES OF SAGE, WHICH IS CALLED SALVIA IN LATIN.

§ 792. Sage is a herb of a hot and dry nature. Boiled in all kinds of food and drink, it is useful in nervous conditions. It is good to take a decoction of it as one's sole drink; adding honey makes it more beneficial for the stomach. If a woman has a dead fetus in the womb, let her boil sage in white wine and drink it cold; she will be safely delivered of her burden. When carefully bruised and applied to a poisoned wound, it will draw out the poison and heal the wound.

If a wound is also full of blood, let the bruised herb be applied to it, and it will cleanse it.

When a man has pain under his rib, let him obtain some sage, boil it on the fire until as hot as he can drink it, and it will cure him.

Also, a decoction in water, or a preparation made with wine, mead, or ale, is an excellent drink for curing dropsy, whooping cough, or headache.

HERE FOLLOW THE VIRTUES OF THE NETTLE.

§ 793. The nettle is a very hot and dry herb. If it is boiled in white wine, strained carefully through linen, left to cool, and drunk morning and night, it will help a man suffering from jaundice.

Take nettle seeds, grind them into a powder, and boil well in spring water, goat's milk, good white wine, or strong

old mead. This potion is good for an old cough, and the colic. It will also strengthen the absorbent and circulating vessels, if salt be added to it.

THE VIRTUES OF THE BLESSED THISTLE (Carduus Benedictus).

§ 794. The blessed thistle is a laxative; when eaten it will help headache and the midriff, and also strengthen the hearing. It strengthens the brain and sight, not only by eating it, but also when the juice is applied to the eye. When juice cannot be obtained, let the powder be taken in water, with the juice dropped into the eye. This is good for removing pooled blood in the eyes. This herb is also a strengthener of the intellect and memory. It is also good for dizziness, and bleeding from the nose and mouth. The powder mixed with honey will promote the clearing of phlegm, strengthen digestion, restore the appetite, ease nausea, and refresh the blood. If the herb is boiled in water and drunk, it will prevent deterioration of the blood and keep it in a healthy condition. If it is eaten it will strengthen limbs weakened by paralysis, as well as the spinal marrow and brain. It will expel the cold humor that weakens the power of the mind and the strength of the body. It will also ease painful bowels, and boiled or drunk with wine, it will break up kidney stones. Whoever drinks it in a male child's urine will be cured of plague and dropsy. It will bring carbuncles to a head, cure cancer and hysteria. The powder will cure hysteria in twelve hours, and if applied to a wound, it will heal it painlessly. If the herb is chewed, it will strengthen the breath. It will cure fever if boiled in wine and drunk warm a quarter of an hour before the onset of the attack, the patient being well covered with clothes so that he may sweat. This

444 PHYSICIANS OF MYDDVAI.

will also cure intermittent, inflammatory, and rheumatic fevers. The powder also taken in warm wine, or some of the distilled water of the herb, will quickly free the patient from every poison affecting the nerves. If the decoction, juice, or distilled water is drunk, and the patient perspires for three hours afterward, it will cure the patient. The powder of the herb, eaten or drunk, will ease pain in the sides and chest. These are the virtues of the blessed thistle.

THE FOLLOWING ARE THE VIRTUES OF CLEAVERS, OR GOOSE GRASS.

§ 795. The juice taken in spring and summer as the sole drink will expel and completely destroy eruptive poison from the blood and humors. This virus is the cause of all eruptions, boils, scalds, scrofula, leprosy, cancer, erysipelas, pneumonia, dropsy, rheumatism, gout, difficulty urinating, all sorts of fevers, pocks of flesh and skin, all watery diseases of the eye, all phlegm of the head or stomach, all white swellings of joints or other parts, every inflamed condition of the blood and humors, every headache attended with fever, every oppression of the chest and stomach or submammary region, every swelling of the legs, feet, or other parts of the body — for there is hardly a disease affecting the human body that is not brought on by an eruptive poison in the blood and humors.

Their juice is obtained as follows. Take the whole herb, leaves, blossoms, and seed included (as the season allows), and pound them together well; then place them in an unglazed earthenware vessel and fill it up without pressing them; then pour over them as much pure spring water as it will hold, and let it stand overnight. Some say it is best that a quarter of the liquid be sea water, or water salted to the same degree as sea water, for the first week of drinking; then, stopping the salt water, it should be taken fresh as the only drink for nine weeks. It is remarkable how strong and healthy you will become in that time.

Gather the herbs in spring and summer and dry them well under the morning sun, turning them so that the sun may

PHYSICIANS OF MYDDVAI. 445

dry them completely; doing this during the day, and bringing them under cover at night. If not dry enough, do this another day, and another again, if in consequence of rain and fog they are not dry enough. Take care not to leave them out in foggy muggy weather, as the whole virtue of the herbs will be destroyed thereby. Gather the leaves, flowers, and seed, and dry them separately, keeping them in an oak chest, or a basket of wheaten straw, covered over well. When required, take the leaves, make an infusion thereof, and drink for three weeks; after that make an infusion of the blossoms, and drink for three weeks; then make an infusion of the seed, and drink for three weeks. Thus you will proceed in God's order, the consistency of nature, and in accord with the constitution and season of the year.

This is the way in which an infusion is made of these herbs: bruise them small with your hands, and fill up an unglazed earthen vessel with them, covering it with boiled running water. Before you do this, cover the herbs with the hair-bottom of a milk strainer, so that the herbs may not get over the edge of the vessel when the water is poured on. Let the vessel stand well covered for six hours, and use the infusion as your sole drink. The herbs should be pressed at night under a press, and the liquid received through a strainer into a clean vessel. It should be drunk warm when going to bed. Should there be any sort of eruption, boil, abscess, ringworm, scab, itching, burning, wound, ulcer, or bruise on your body, wash it with a lotion of the herbs, either juice or decoction. If the disease is considerable, apply the bruised herbs directly to it. This treatment with potions and local applications has healed scrofula, the skin disease called in Latin lepra, and cancer, even when it had destroyed the flesh down to the bones.

Take also the seed of the herbs when ripe, and dry in an oven after baking two or three times. When dry enough, powder them in a stone mortar, keeping the powder in a glass bottle, well covered; carry this with you on a journey, and

446 PHYSICIANS OF MYDDVAI.

Take a spoonful in clear water three times a day. It will protect you from all kinds of ailments, and will serve as food in case of necessity. It is also good to do the same with mallow seed, using it in the same way.

THE FOLLOWING ARE THE VIRTUES OF THE MISTLETOE.

§ 796. Mistletoe most frequently grows on the apple tree or the hawthorn, and occasionally on the oak, which is to be preferred, though it is an excellent plant wherever it grows. Its property is to strengthen the body more than any other plant. Gather it at Christmas time, when the berries are fully ripe, and pick the berries from the branches. Pour boiling water over them, cover the vessel in which they are contained, and set it near the fire so that it may simmer for a night and a day. It should then be strained through a hair cloth into a clean vessel. Let the leaves and sprigs of the plant be bruised small and laid on a hot baking stone, where they should be thoroughly roasted, being stirred continuously so that they do not burn. When sufficiently roasted, they should be powdered, half of this powder being set aside for use, and the remainder burned to fine ashes. The powder and the ashes should be carefully preserved in separate glass vials.

In any case of bodily weakness, whether in the nerves, joints, back, head, brain, stomach, heart, lungs, or kidneys, take three spoonfuls of the decoction and mix with boiling water, ale, mead, or milk. Then add to a good draft of this a spoonful of the powder, which should be drunk in the morning on an empty stomach. Half as much should be taken last thing at night. It is good for any kind of disease of the brain, nerves, and back, epilepsy, mania, or any mental infirmity, paralysis, all weakness of joints, sight, hearing, or the senses. It will promote fertility, the begetting of children, and restrain seminal flux. The man who takes a spoonful of it daily in his drink will enjoy uninterrupted health, strength of body, and manly vigor.

* i.e. Misseltoe.

PHYSICIANS OF MYDDVAI. 447

The same result will follow if he takes a spoonful of the decoction in his drink daily.

If a patient is ill of strangury, flatulent dyspepsia, or dropsy, let him take a spoonful of the ashes in drink three times a day, and when possible let him drink an infusion of the plant, either freshly gathered or dried. It will preserve and cure him.

When the plant grows nearby, he need only gather the berries fresh daily as needed for a decoction, and the plant fresh for an infusion. But when it can only be obtained from afar, let it be used as directed, keeping the plants dry in the house all through the year, gathering them in summer, winter, and spring, as they can be obtained.

The best places to obtain them are Monmouthshire, Somersetshire, Brecknockshire, and Shropshire. The best time to gather them is in the depth of winter, from the feast of St. Andrew to Candlemas; and it is also good to gather the green herb from the feast of St. James to the first of November. To obtain their ashes, it is best that they be burned while still green, before they have lost their sap.

THE FOLLOWING ARE THE VIRTUES OF THE OAK.

§ 797. The oak will supply a variety of remedies for all diseases stemming from weakness in the nerves, spinal marrow, and brain. Remedies are obtained from the oak in a variety of ways.

Take fresh chips of oak and soak them in running water until their virtues are extracted; then take them out and replace with fresh chips, treating them as before. After doing this nine times, boil the liquid down to half, add a pound of honey for every two gallons, and allow it to ferment. A quantity of mistletoe decoction equal to the amount of honey, or any lesser quantity, may be added if any is on hand; but if not, it will still be a very excellent drink, and is called Oak Beer. It is the best drink of all for strengthening the body, constitution, nerves, brain, and spinal marrow. It will also cure diseases that arise from weakness, provided a good draught is drunk every morning on an empty stomach.

448 PHYSICIANS OF MYDDVAI.

The inner bark of the oak is an excellent tonic. It should be kept, dried and powdered, as well as simply well dried, so that it may be at hand when needed, in either form. It is excellent when taken in ale, or as a decoction, in all cases of debility, in all fevers, whether sustained or inflammatory, in tertian or quartan intermittent fevers, or when eruptive poison is present in the blood or humors. A decoction of the fresh bark boiled in ale, or the milk of cows or goats, is very good for the same diseases.

Take ripe acorns, roast them until very crisp, and keep them in a well-covered oak vessel. Take a spoonful with your drink night and morning. Whenever a man or woman suffers from functional or seminal weakness, three tablespoonfuls of this powder should be boiled in a good draught of goat's or cow's milk, then drunk mixed with honey morning and night, for it will cure the complaint. It is useful for all the previously mentioned diseases, for uterine hemorrhage in women, for eruptions of all kinds in men, and for diseased lungs. It makes an excellent everyday food (mixed with well-baked wheaten bread) for all weak persons, or those subject to lung complaints, or bodily or constitutional debility of any kind.

Malt some acorns and make ale from them. It is the best and most healthful ale of any kind, and an excellent tonic in cases of debility or diseases arising from it.

Gather oak leaves in August or September, dry them well, and keep them covered. If applied to any bruised skin or weeping sore, they will heal it.

Take roasted acorns, or the inner bark roasted, ground together with bread grain, and make bread from it. This bread is the best of any for strengthening a person's body and removing all complaints caused by winter cold or dampness.

THE FOLLOWING ARE THE VIRTUES OF THE VERVAIN.

§ 798. Should you be affected with scrofula, take a decoction or infusion of vervain, gathering the entire plant when it is in seed; roast it well and powder it. Keep this very

THE FOLLOWING IS AN EXPLANATION OF THE FOUR ELEMENTS OF MAN; FROM WHICH COME THE FOUR CONSTITUTIONS OR TEMPERAMENTS OF MAN, NAMELY, THE SANGUINE, THE CHOLERIC, THE PHLEGMATIC, AND THE MELANCHOLIC.

Section 799. How to recognize persons of a sanguine constitution. A person of sanguine constitution will be naturally fat, but not simply fat, as that would indicate a cold nature; for as Avicenna* says, an abundance of flesh indicates a hot nature; and plenty of flesh is the result of an abundance of blood, as Avicenna says. Every ruddy, red-haired, spare man is of a sanguine temperament, as Galen says. Sanguine men will be cheerful, and fond of listening to stories and entertainment, and for the same reason they are lacking in self-control, and prone to giving way to their animal instincts. They will

also drink wine jovially. A sanguine man will eat the best food, for sanguine people seek what corresponds most closely with their nature. A sanguine man will also be inclined to play, for his blood naturally tends toward cheerfulness. He will also be fair-complexioned, by virtue of his constitution, eloquent in speech, and quick to acquire all knowledge, arts, and profound systems of thought. He will be poetically inclined, delighting in imagination and ambitious projects. He will not easily be provoked to anger; he will be generous, not covetous, amiable, affectionate in behavior, and kind in conduct. He will have a ruddy complexion, for as Avicenna observes, a ruddy skin indicates an abundance of blood. This should be a clear, transparent red, not a livid red, as seen in those whose faces are florid from drinking to excess or living on a vegetable diet; for such a complexion indicates lepra, scurvy, or an excess of humor and blood. He will sing sweetly and pleasantly, he will delight in music and in the company of singers, and in the merry and poetical. He will delight in the harp and all instrumental music; he will be quick and industrious in work or on errands; he will also be brave and confident, owing to the heat of his blood, and gentlemanly in his bearing, owing to the activity of his circulation. When uneducated, he will tend to become conceited about his own abilities, as well as contrary, impertinent, and disagreeable, as a result of the over-excited state of his blood. He will be more inclined to focus his mind and act on what is near rather than distant. He will also learn more from natural genius than from study, and will be satirical and curt in what he says or does. He is apt to laugh and be jolly without reason, beyond the excited and untameable tendency of the sanguine temperament.

TO RECOGNISE THE PHLEGMATIC TEMPERAMENT.

§ 800. One who is of a phlegmatic temperament will have brown hair, because his constitution is relatively weak. In the second place, phlegmatic persons will be short and fat,

PHYSICIANS OF MYDDVAI. 451

As their natural strength is not sufficient to permit them to continue growing, they will also be less energetic than persons of other temperaments, due to their coldness, which will also make them more sleepy. They will be a prudent people, but also idle — for just as heat makes a man light and lively, cold makes him heavy and lazy. Phlegmatic people will also be fat due to bodily impurity. They will be sluggish in mind, sleepy, or inclined to sleep a great deal. If educated, they will be intelligent and will achieve what is expected of them; but because of their sluggishness, they will perform only indifferently in all competitive efforts and will soon give up. Their memory will be poor, and they will not love except out of selfish motives. They will not seek merriment, song, or jollity, and even when they possess knowledge, they will be found lacking in genius. But when there is a mixture of the sanguine in their constitution, one may often find such a person wise in knowledge and of strong genius, being patient, long-suffering, and discreet. He will not love contention, mimicry, or flippancy, because he will not value anything except what is fitting and substantial.

TO RECOGNIZE THE VAPOURISH CONSTITUTION, AND THE PERSONS WHO ARE OF THAT TEMPERAMENT.

§ 801. He who is of a vapourish or choleric constitution will be impatient, due to an excess of heat that inclines him toward recklessness. A person of this constitution will be very ambitious for superiority, dignity, and authority over others, inasmuch as natural heat inclines the mind toward folly. Vapourish persons will also have an ease in acquiring learning due to the heat of bile, but they will not retain what they have learned. They will also be high-spirited — that is, they will not patiently endure injustice, because of their heat. They will aspire to great eminence, official position, and social elevation. A choleric man will be as lustful as a goat,

452 PHYSICIANS OF MYDDVAI.

Passion, rather than love, will guide him in all things. He will be a deceiver, quick to anger over trifles, showing in this the heat of vapor and the boiling of the blood around the heart. He will be cunning, quick, and reckless in his plans and policies, more notable for his violence than for any consistency in his actions or thoughts. He will be slender in his limbs, ungracious in his manner, and yellow as saffron in his complexion. As Avicenna says, this complexion indicates arrogance — a person of slender body and limbs, one who sees faults in others where none exist, yet is blind to his own imperfections. He will be kind to those who honor him, cold and haughty to those who do not, and vengeful toward those who wrong or falsely injure him. The phlegmatic character cannot be mixed with this constitution; and if it could be, a sanguine temperament would render it unfaithful and capricious. Of the four constitutions of man, this is the least capable of improvement. Rhys the Physician has called this the vaporous temperament, as it is caused by the boiling of the heart and the bitterness of the bile in man.

THE FOLLOWING ARE INSTRUCTIONS FOR RECOGNIZING THE NATURE AND CONSTITUTION OF MELANCHOLY, AND THE TEMPERAMENT OF THOSE WHO ARE MELANCHOLIC.

§ 802. A person of melancholic constitution will be surly and unmanly, as if at war with himself. Most melancholic people will also be sad and unsociable due to their cold nature. They will be studious, meditative, and thoughtful, and inclined to seek solitude. Because of the dryness of the brain, their sleep will not be sound, being broken and disturbed by dreams. Among studious minds, their memory will be good. They will be difficult to please, envious, covetous, prone to wrongdoing through moral weakness, and little able to follow through on their good intentions — consequently unreliable in payments and prone to dishonesty. A melancholic man will be a great reader, abstemious, fearful, and his complexion will be earth-toned; if it has a shade of green, this will indicate dignity, as the wise Cassius says. All men of this

PHYSICIANS OF MYDDVAI. 453

People of this sort will be exposed to extremes in all things; if sad and sorrowful they will be exceedingly so; if joyful, there will be no limit to their joy. They love singing in solitude, and from a solitary place, to listen to song and harp. They like to speak their minds about others, but in no way to reveal their own inner feelings. They are lovers of song and curious research, but do not much care to show it. They tend to cultivate the arts and sciences, taking care to understand what they are doing, and to be careful about what they say and do. If there is a sanguine element in the mixture, they will be found to be a superior class of men. If the choleric element dominates, they will be bitter, surly, and most disagreeable men. If there is a phlegmatic admixture, there will be a tendency toward insanity and mental conflict. This class of men will be slender of body and limb. Many a poet will be found of this constitution, and they will often exhibit excessive love and excessive hate.

There are four principal exciting causes of fever and disease in the human body, namely:

1. Fever, brought on by an excess of heat or cold.

2. Eruptive poison in the blood or humors, produced by irregularities in eating and drinking.

3. Obstructions in the stomach, veins, or other hollow vessels of the body, so that food, drink, blood, or humors cannot pass through as normal.

4. A boil, carbuncle, or plague, caused by the entry of poison into the system. From these four arise all fevers and diseases affecting the human body, and it is through the use of active remedies that they are cured.

USEFUL THINGS.

The following are things useful to be known by every Physician, and by every head of a household:

Infusion: Pouring water or another fluid in a boiling state over herbs or whatever other ingredient may be required.
Decoction: Boiling the herbs or ingredients in the water or fluid required.
Pottage or Porridge: Pouring boiling or cold water, or another suitable fluid, over herbs or other ingredients, leaving them to stand, then straining under a press.
Soakage: Pouring cold or boiling water, or another fluid, over any substance capable of being affected by it, so that it becomes incorporated with what is poured upon it.
Confection: Fluids mixed with powders or other substances suitable for administering as a drink.
Potion: A drink or fluid prepared according to the art of medicine.
Essence: An amorphous or fragrant substance, which may be taken as a drink by mouth, or introduced into the nostrils, ear,* rectum, or another part of the body.
Electuary: Substances incorporated into a dough so as to be eaten.
Constitution: The disposition present in a person, or other living being, or herb, or other matter; being their virtue, inherent property, or nature.
Pills: Medical substances combined and formed into small balls so as to be swallowed in one gulp.
Bath:† An infusion or decoction in which the patient or his limb is to be placed.
Fomentation: To be applied as a wash to an injury, whether hot or cold, as required.
Regimen: Food and drink as regulated by medical advice.

* External ear.

THE ESSENTIALS OF A PHYSICIAN.

These things should be in the possession of a Physician: and then follow the characteristics which should distinguish him, which are called the Essentials of a Physician.

1. A lancet to bleed or open an abscess, and also a slightly larger knife.

2. A steel or silver spatula to spread plaster.

3. A pipe and bladder for injecting into the urinary organs or rectum.

4. His plasters, ointments, pills, powders, and potions, carefully stored to meet any need or occasion.

5. A garden of trees and herbs, where plants that do not grow naturally everywhere may be cultivated, and where foreign trees and plants that need shelter and care before they can thrive in Wales may be grown.

6. He should also keep on hand his dry herbs, roots, seeds, and barks, so they may be available in winter and at other times when they cannot be obtained growing or above ground.

7. He should also have on hand his honey, wax, pitch, rosin, gums, oil, tallow, grease, lard, marble slab, ale, wine, mead, distillations, and other such articles as may be needed.

8. He should also have on hand his mortars, strainer, press, stoneware, glassware, wooden vessels, fire utensils, and containers for keeping articles, whether of glass, earthenware, or silver, with good covers, so that the drugs do not become inert or poisonous through poor storage, carelessness, or ignorance.

9. He should also have weights and balances on hand, made of silver or tin, so that nothing harmful gets into the drugs. All his liquid or fluid measures should likewise be made of silver or tin for the same reason. The same applies to his surgical instruments generally, with the exception of lancets, cutting scalpels, and probing needles.

10. All his weights and measures, whether for solids or liquids, should be of guaranteed weight and capacity, so he can be certain of the proportions of all ingredients, and neither exceed nor fall short of the required quantity, as either error would render the remedy ineffective or poisonous.

11. He should also possess authorized Books of Art approved by a master, so that he may be skilled in the judgment and knowledge of the wise and able Physicians who came before him and who wrote with authority in Welsh, Latin, and Arabic.

12. He should also be declared competent to practice by the authority of the wise and learned masters of the art.

13. He should be a kind man, gentle, mild, meek, intelligent, wise, and gentlemanly in action and deed, in word and conduct, being careful never to embarrass those he has to examine, particularly when examining women.
